Cooking: 20–30 minutes
Total: 40–50 minutes | Difficulty = 2 | Image = [[File:Miyan kuka 02.jpg|300px]] }} {{recipe}} '''Miyan kuka''' ("baobab leaf soup") is a Northern Nigerian [[Cookbook:Soup|soup]] prepared with dried ground baobab leaves (kuka). This soup is paired with [[Cookbook:Tuwo Shinkafa (Nigerian Mashed Rice)|tuwo shinkafa]] or [[Cookbook:Tuwo Masara (Nigerian Corn Fufu)|tuwo masara]]. ==Ingredients== * 2 large [[Cookbook:Dryfish|dried]] [[Cookbook:Catfish|catfish]] * 1 large [[Cookbook:Iru|dawa dawa]] lump * 2 handfuls [[Cookbook:Ground Crayfish|ground crayfish]] * Atarugu ([[Cookbook:Habanero|habanero]] pepper) * 1 [[Cookbook:Kilogram|kg]] [[Cookbook:Beef|cow]] rib * 2 large [[Cookbook:Bouillon Cube|stock cube]] * [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]], to taste * 1 [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], cut in chunks * 3 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] kuka ([[Cookbook:Baobab|baobab]] leaf) powder * 2 cooking spoons [[Cookbook:Palm Oil|palm oil]] ==Equipment== *Cooking pot *Wooden spoon or whisk *Blender or mortar and pestle *Knife *Bowl *Sieve (optional) ==Procedure== # Soak the dried fish in cold water. Debone when soft. # Grind the crayfish with dawadawa. Pound the pepper. # Cook the cow ribs with water, stock cube, salt, and onions until the meat is tender. Remove the onions, then the beef, reserving the stock in the pot. # Stir the kuka powder into the reserved stock until smooth, with no lumps. # Stir in pounded pepper, crayfish and dawa dawa mixture, and palm oil. # Add the deboned fish, cover, and cook 5 minutes over medium heat. # Stir in beef, and add salt to taste. Cook for 2 minutes. # Serve with tuwo shinkafa or tuwo masara. ==Notes, tips, and variations== *Add the kuka powder gradually to avoid lumps. Too much kuka powder can make the soup bitter. *Continuous stirring improves the smooth texture. *The soup often tastes better after resting for several hours or overnight. *Palm oil gives the soup a richer aroma and appearance. title: Cookbook:Miyan Ridi (Nigerian Sesame Soup)
text:
__notoc__
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Nigerian recipes
| Servings = 2-3
| Difficulty = 2
}}

{{recipe}}

'''Miya Ridi''' is a traditional toasted sesame seed soup popular among the Hausa people of Northern Nigeria. Rich in flavor and often served with tuwo or other local swallows, it is a nutritious dish commonly prepared during special occasions or family meals.

==Ingredients==
* [[Cookbook:Beef|Beef]] (any type), cut in pieces
* 1 large [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* [[Cookbook:Bouillon Cube|Seasoning cube]]
* Tatashe (red [[Cookbook:Bell Pepper|bell pepper]]), [[Cookbook:Puréeing|blended]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] toasted [[Cookbook:Sesame Seed|sesame seeds]] (ridi)
* 3 [[Cookbook: Cooking Spoon|cooking spoons]] [[Cookbook:Palm Oil|palm oil]]
* [[Cookbook: Onion|Onion]], [[Cookbook:Slicing|sliced]]
* 2 medium-sized dried smoked fish
* Alayyahu ([[Cookbook:Spinach|spinach]])

== Ingredients ==
* 500 g [[Cookbook:Beef|beef]], cut into bite-sized pieces
* 1 large [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], chopped
* 2 [[Cookbook:Bouillon Cube|seasoning cubes]] (e.g., Maggi)
* 2 large tatashe ([[Cookbook:Bell Pepper|red bell pepper]]), blended
* 2 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] toasted [[Cookbook:Sesame Seed|sesame seeds]] (ridi), blended into a paste
* 3 tablespoons [[Cookbook:Palm Oil|palm oil]]
* 1 small [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], sliced
* 2 medium-sized dried smoked fish, cleaned and deboned
* 1 chopped alayyahu ([[Cookbook:Spinach|spinach]])
* [[Cookbook:Water|Water]], as needed

== Procedure ==
# In a pot, boil the beef with the chopped onion, seasoning cubes, and a little water until the meat is tender.
# Blend the toasted sesame seeds into a smooth paste using a blender or grinding stone.
# In a separate pot, heat the palm oil over medium heat. Add the sliced onion and blended red bell pepper, then fry for 5–7 minutes until fragrant.
# Add the cooked beef and some of the beef stock. Stir in the smoked fish and simmer for 5 minutes.
# Add the ground sesame seed paste. Stir continuously to avoid lumps, and cook for about 10 minutes. Add water as needed to reach desired consistency.
# Add the chopped spinach, stir, and turn off the heat after 1–2 minutes.
# Serve hot with [[Cookbook:Tuwo Shinkafa (Nigerian Mashed Rice)|tuwo shinkafa]], [[Cookbook:Pounded Yam|pounded yam]], wheat, or other [[Cookbook:Swallow|swallow]] of choice.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* Groundnut (peanut) paste can be added along with sesame paste for a richer flavor.
* You can substitute spinach with ugu or kale depending on availability.
* For a vegetarian version, omit the meat and fish, and add mushrooms or tofu.

* 800 g cored and [[Cookbook:Slicing|sliced]] apples (from about 12 large apples)s
* 2 packets shortcrust [[Cookbook:Pastry Dough|pastry dough]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Kilogram|kg]] lean [[Cookbook:Pork|pork]] mince
* 100 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]]

== Special equipment ==
* 3 greased [[Cookbook:Muffin Pan|muffin tins]]

== Procedure ==
# Preheat [[Cookbook:Oven|oven]] to 150 °C (300 °F).
# In a pot, bring the sugar, wine, cider, orange, and lemon juice to a [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]]. Add mace, nutmeg, and cinnamon. Split the vanilla pod and scrape seeds into pot. Discard vanilla pod. 
# Stir in sliced apples and fruit mix.
# Grease the muffin tins, and line with pastry dough to make tartlet cases. Trim to fit.
# Place cases into oven, and [[Cookbook:Baking|bake]] until lightly golden. Remove from oven and let cool.
# Melt butter in a pan. Add minced pork, and [[Cookbook:Sautéing|sauté]] until browned.
# Remove cinnamon stick from the fruit mixture, and mix in the pork.
# Using a tablespoon, fill tartlet cases with the filling—it will probably be mounded.
# If desired, trim with excess pastry.
# Bake each tray at 120 °C (250 °F) for half an hour.

text:
__NOTOC__{{Recipe summary

{{Recipe}}

This recipe is for a traditional miso soup. [[Cookbook:Wakame|Wakame]] with [[Cookbook:Tofu|tofu]] is a standard and popular combination, especially at restaurants.

== Ingredients ==

=== Broth ===
* 90–94% by volume [[Cookbook:Dashi|dashi]] (consider using instant dashi mix)
* 6–10% by volume [[Cookbook:Miso|miso]] (red, white, or a combination)

=== Garnish ===
Any 2–3 of the following items that contrast in color, flavor, buoyancy, shape, texture, etc:

* Finely sliced and [[Cookbook:Deep Fat Fry|deep-fried]] [[Cookbook:Tofu|tofu]] (agedashi tofu)
* Cubed raw silky [[Cookbook:Tofu|tofu]] ('''recommended''')
* [[Cookbook:Wakame|Wakame]] seaweed ('''recommended''')
* [[Cookbook:Konbu|Konbu]] (kelp), perhaps left over from making dashi
* [[Cookbook:Spinach|Spinach]]
* Sliced [[Cookbook:Scallion|scallion]] ('''recommended''')
* Grated [[Cookbook:Daikon|daikon]] radish
* Boiled and finely cubed [[Cookbook:Potato|potato]]
* [[Cookbook:Clam|Clams]] (asari or shijimi)
* Grated [[Cookbook:Eggplant|eggplant]]
* [[Cookbook:Shrimp|Shrimp]]
* [[Cookbook:Mushroom|Mushrooms]]

== Procedure ==
# Put dashi in a pot.
# Add any garnish that needs cooking.
# Heat the dashi, letting it [[Cookbook:Simmer|simmer]] to cook any garnish that needs cooking. Do not bring to a rolling [[Cookbook:Boil|boil]], as this degrades the flavor.
# Add any garnish that does not need cooking, and remove from heat.
# Add the miso to the soup. Avoid boiling the miso; some nuances of the flavor will be lost.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* While certainly a traditional food, miso soup is also suited to modern interpretations. Using oil leftover from frying bacon and adding caramelized onion and cabbage produces a soup notably different from the traditional variety, and can add new interest to a classic dish. A small quantity of freshly ground black pepper added just before serving rounds out this method very well.

title: Cookbook:Milk Toast II
text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Bread recipes
| Difficulty = 2
}}

{{Recipe}}

'''Milk toast''' is a [[Cookbook:Breakfast|breakfast]] food consisting of [[Cookbook:Toast|toasted]] [[Cookbook:Bread|bread]] dipped in [[Cookbook:Milk|milk]]. Milk toast was a popular food throughout the late 19th century and early 20th century, especially for young children and for the ailing, for whom the food was thought to be soothing and easy to digest. Although not as popular today, milk toast is still considered a comfort food.

This recipe comes from the 1918 edition of ''The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book'' by Fannie Farmer, a famous home-cooking author and instructor of the early 20th century.

== Ingredients ==
* 1 [[Cookbook:Pint|pint]] (570 [[Cookbook:Milliliter|ml]]) [[Cookbook:Scald|scalded]] [[Cookbook:Milk|milk]]
* ½ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]]
* 4 tablespoons cold [[Cookbook:Water|water]]
* 2 ½ tablespoons bread [[Cookbook:Flour|flour]]
* 6 slices dry toast

== Procedure ==

# Gradually add cold water to flour to make a smooth, thin paste. 
# Add paste to milk, stirring constantly until thickened.
# Cover, and cook 20 minutes; then, add salt and butter in small pieces. 
# Dip slices of toast separately in sauce; when soft, remove to serving dish. Pour remaining sauce over all.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* Although both above recipes call for salt, milk toast may also be made sweet by the omission of salt and pepper and the addition, instead, of [[Cookbook:Sugar|sugar]]. Other optional ingredients for sweet versions include [[Cookbook:Cinnamon|cinnamon]], [[Cookbook:Honey|honey]] or a touch of [[Cookbook:Vanilla|vanilla]], but piquant and exotic ingredients should be avoided, as the primary purpose of milk toast is to provide a food soothing to the palate and to the digestion.
* [[Cookbook:Cornstarch|Corn starch]] may be substituted for flour.

text:

{{Recipe}}

== Ingredients ==

* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] white [[Cookbook:Vinegar|vinegar]]
* 50 [[Cookbook:Milliliter|ml]] (¼ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]]) [[Cookbook:Vegetable oil|vegetable oil]]
* 2 tbsp [[Cookbook:Water|water]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] dried [[Cookbook:Thyme|thyme]]
* 1 tsp [[Cookbook:Garlic Powder|garlic powder]]
* 1 tsp [[Cookbook:Coriander|coriander]] powder
* 1 tsp [[Cookbook:Cumin|cumin]] powder
* ½ tsp [[Cookbook:Cayenne Pepper|cayenne pepper]]
* ½ tsp [[Cookbook:Paprika|paprika]] powder
* 1 tsp [[Cookbook:Onion Powder|onion powder]]
* 1 tsp ground [[Cookbook:Pepper|black pepper]]
* ¼ tsp ground [[Cookbook:Allspice|allspice]]
* 1 tsp [[Cookbook:Garlic Powder|garlic]] paste
* 1 tsp [[Cookbook:Ginger|ginger]] paste
* [[Cookbook:Beef|Beef]] sirloin steak, in 1-[[Cookbook:Inch|inch]] cubes
* 80 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] [[Cookbook:Cilantro|fresh coriander]], finely [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]

== Special equipment ==

* Metal [[Cookbook:Skewer|skewers]]
* [[Cookbook:Grill|Grill]]
* Ziplock bag

== Procedure ==

# [[Cookbook:Whisk|Whisk]] together the vinegar, oil, water, thyme, spices, ginger paste, and garlic paste to make a [[Cookbook:Marinating|marinade]].
# Add the meat and [[Cookbook:Mixing#Tossing|toss]] well, then transfer everything to a large ziplock bag. Seal the bag and marinate in the refrigerator for 24–48 hours.
# Take the meat out of the refrigerator, and give it at least an hour to come to room temperature.
# Thread the meat on the skewers.
# Preheat a charcoal grill for some time.
# Grease the grill grate, and place the skewers on the grate. Cook until medium-done (internal temperature of 65°C / 145°F).
# Serve hot with fresh coriander.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* If you would like to use wood skewers, soak them in water for an hour before using. This prevents them from burning.
* You could also [[Cookbook:Broiling|broil]] the skewers in the oven instead of grilling.

title: Cookbook:Miyan Lalo (Hausa Jute Leaf Soup)
text:
__NOTOC__{{Recipe summary
| Category = Soup recipes
| Servings = 2–3
| Difficulty = 3
| Image = 
}}

{{Recipe}}

[[File:Tree of Baobab.jpg|thumb|Tree of Baobab]]

'''Miyan Lalo''' is a traditional jute leaf soup commonly eaten by the Hausa people of Northern Nigeria. It is similar in preparation and texture to the Yoruba dish known as ewedu soup.

== Ingredients ==
* 3 medium pieces of [[Cookbook:Meat and Poultry|meat]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoons]] [[Cookbook:Dehydrated Broth|stock cube]] (e.g., Maggi)
* ½ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] dried ground [[Cookbook:Chile pepper|chile pepper]] (adjust to taste)
* 1 large [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], chopped
* 2 bunches of fresh [[Cookbook:Jute|jute]] (lalo) leaves, chopped
* 1 small piece of [[Cookbook:Potash|potash]] (kanwa)
* 2 medium pieces of [[Cookbook:Iru|daddawa]] (fermented locust bean), pounded
* [[Cookbook: Water|Water]] (as needed for boiling)

== Equipment ==
* [[Cookbook:Pots and Pans|Pot]]
* [[Cookbook:Stovetop|Stovetop]]
* [[Cookbook:Knife|Knife]]
* [[Cookbook:Blender|Blender]] or grinding stone 
* [[Cookbook: Mixing Bowl|Bowl]]

== Procedure ==
# In a pot, boil the meat with the stock cube, half of the chopped onion, and just enough water to cover the meat. Cook until the meat is tender.
# Add the chopped jute leaves and potash. Cook for 5–10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
# Blend the remaining onion with the chile pepper and a small amount of water to form a purée. Add this mixture to the pot along with the pounded daddawa.
# Stir well and simmer for another 2 minutes, then remove from heat. Serve hot with tuwo (e.g., Tuwon Semo, Tuwon Masara, Tuwon Shinkafa, Semovita or Fufu).

== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* You can use frozen jute leaves or molokhia as a substitute if fresh lalo is unavailable.
* Ground crayfish or seasoning oil may be added for extra flavor depending on personal preference.

title: Cookbook:Moambe (Palm Nut Soup)
text:
__NOTOC__
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Soup recipes
| Difficulty = 3
}}

{{Recipe}}

'''Moambe''' is a delicious and popular dish from Central and West Africa. This rich and flavorful soup is made from palm nuts and typically includes an assortment of meats, vegetables, and spices. It is often served with a side of fufu, rice, or plantains.

== Ingredients ==

* 2 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] [[Cookbook:Oil Palm Fruit|palm nuts]] (either fresh, frozen, or canned)
* 2–3 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] red [[Cookbook:Palm Oil|palm oil]]
* 1 medium-sized [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 2–3 cloves of [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Mince|minced]]
* 1–2 pounds [[Cookbook:Meat and Poultry|meat]] ([[Cookbook:Chicken|chicken]], [[Cookbook:Beef|beef]], or [[Cookbook:Goat|goat]]), cut into bite-sized pieces
* 1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] ground [[Cookbook:Ginger|ginger]]
* 1 teaspoon [[Cookbook:Garlic Powder|ground garlic]]
* 1 teaspoon ground [[Cookbook:Pepper|black pepper]]
* 1 cup fresh or frozen [[Cookbook:Okra|okra]], chopped
* 1–2 cups pumpkin or [[Cookbook:Spinach|spinach]] leaves, chopped
* 1 [[Cookbook:Dryfish|smoked fish]] (optional), deboned and flaked
* 1–2 scotch bonnet or habanero [[Cookbook:Chiles|peppers]], deseeded and chopped (adjust to your desired spiciness)
* 1 teaspoon [[Cookbook:Ground Crayfish|ground crayfish]] (optional)

== Equipment ==

* Large cooking pot
* [[Cookbook:Blender|Blender]] or [[Cookbook:Food Processor|food processor]]
* Wooden spoon or ladle
* [[Cookbook:Knife|Knife]] for chopping
* [[Cookbook:Cutting Board|Cutting board]]

== Procedure ==

# If using fresh palm nuts, crack them open and remove the kernels.
# Place the kernels in a pot, cover them with water, and bring to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]]. [[Cookbook:Simmer|Simmer]] for 30 minutes to soften the nuts.
# Drain the nuts and transfer them to a blender or food processor. Add a cup of water and blend until smooth. Strain the mixture through a fine-mesh [[Cookbook:Sieve|sieve]] to remove any remaining solids. Set aside.
# In the same pot, heat the red palm oil over medium heat. Add the chopped onions and minced garlic. [[Cookbook:Sautéing|Sauté]] until fragrant and translucent.
# Add the meat pieces and cook until browned on all sides.
# Season with ground ginger, ground garlic, ground black pepper, and salt. Stir well to coat the meat evenly.
# Pour the strained palm nut mixture into the pot with the meat. Stir well to combine. Add enough water to achieve your desired consistency. Moambe is typically thick, so adjust accordingly.
# Cover the pot and let the soup simmer on low heat for about 30 minutes to allow the flavors to meld together.
# Add the chopped okra, pumpkin or spinach leaves, and flaked smoked fish (if using). Stir gently to combine.
# Add the chopped scotch bonnet or habanero peppers, adjusting the quantity to suit your taste.
# Sprinkle in the ground crayfish (if using) and stir again. Continue simmering the soup for an additional 10–15 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
# Taste the soup and adjust the salt and spices according to your preference. Once the flavors have melded and the soup has thickened, it is ready to be served.

== Note, tips, and variations ==

* The quantities of ingredients and cooking times can be adjusted based on your personal preference and the number of servings you intend to make.

* 25 g gula melaka [[Cookbook:Palm Sugar|palm sugar]], broken into small pieces

# Combine the cassava, coconut, and salt to form a [[Cookbook:Dough|dough]].

# Insert a piece of the sugar into the pocket, then pinch the dough around it to fully enclose it.
# Roll the finished dumpling in your hands to shape it into a ball again.
# Heat enough oil for shallow- or deep-[[Cookbook:Frying|frying]] in a [[Cookbook:Frying Pan|skillet]] or pot over medium heat. If you're monitoring the temperature, 350°F (180°C) is a good target.
# Gently place the dough balls in the oil, working in batches if needed to avoid crowding the pan. Fry on all sides, turning as necessary, until golden brown all over and cooked through.
# Use a slotted spoon or spider to remove the fritters from the oil. Drain them on a [[Cookbook:Cooling Rack|rack]] or [[Cookbook:Paper Towel|paper towels]].

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* The cassava and coconut should be very finely grated in order to properly combine them into a dough—large flakes won't work.

title: Cookbook:Miyan Kubewa (Okra Soup)
text:
__NOTOC__{{Recipe summary | Category = Soup recipes | Servings = 2–3 | Time = Preparation: 15–20 minutes
Cooking: 20–30 minutes
Total: 40–50 minutes | Difficulty = 3 | Image = [[file:Okro soup.jpg|300px]] }} {{Recipe}} '''Miyan kuɓewa''' is a popular soup in Hausa cuisine made primarily from okra. Known for its viscous texture and rich flavor, it is widely prepared across Northern Nigeria and other parts of West Africa. The dish is typically enjoyed with traditional starch-based swallows such as tuwo shinkafa (rice flour paste), tuwo masara (maize meal), or tuwo dawa (guinea corn paste). == Ingredients == * 500 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] [[Cookbook:Beef|beef]], [[Cookbook:Goat|goat]], or assorted meat (optional: cow tripe, kidney, or liver) * 1 medium [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]] * 2–3 [[Cookbook:Dehydrated Broth|seasoning cubes]] * [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]] (to taste) * Water (as needed) * 1–2 [[Cookbook:Each|ea]]. [[Cookbook:Dryfish|smoked fish or dried fish]] (optional) * 1–2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] [[Cookbook:Dawadawa|ground locust beans (''dawadawa'')]] * 2–3 tablespoons [[Cookbook:Palm Oil|palm oil]] * 2 cups fresh chopped or grated [[Cookbook:Okra|okra]] (or 1½ cups dried okra) * 2 tablespoons [[Cookbook:Ground Crayfish|ground crayfish]] * Fresh or dried ground [[Cookbook:Scotch Bonnet Chile|Scotch bonnet chile]] (to taste) ==Equipment== *Cooking pot *Knife *Chopping board *Blender or mortar and pestle *Wooden spoon *Bowl == Procedure == # In a pot, combine your cleaned meat, chopped onions, seasoning cubes, and a pinch of salt. Add a little water and [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] until the meat is cooked through and tender to your taste. This can take a while for tough cuts of meat. # If using smoked or dried fish, add it along with the ground locust beans (''dawadawa''). Allow it to simmer for 5–10 minutes. # Pour in the palm oil and stir well. Let it cook for a few minutes to combine the flavors. # Stir in the okra. If using dried okra, you may need to add some extra water. Stir continuously to encourage the characteristic "draw" (slippery texture). # Sprinkle in the ground crayfish and pepper. Adjust salt and seasoning to taste. # Allow the soup to simmer for another 5–10 minutes. Avoid overcooking the okra to maintain its texture. == Notes, tips, and variations == * Fresh okra gives a better texture, but dried okra is more convenient for storage and travel. * ''Dawadawa'' adds a unique, pungent aroma typical of Hausa soups. * Crayfish is optional but adds depth of flavor, especially if fish is not used. title: Cookbook:Miyan Taushe (Hausa Pumpkin Soup)
text:
__notoc__
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Soup recipes
| Servings = 2–3
| Time = 45–55 minutes
| Difficulty = 2
| Image = [[File:Miyan taushe 03.jpg|300px]]
}}

{{Recipe}}

'''Miyan taushe''' is a traditional, popular soup in Hausa homes, especially during festive seasons or when pumpkins are in season. It reflects the Hausa people's creative use of local ingredients to prepare nourishing, flavorful meals. It is rich, slightly sweet, and often flavored with groundnut paste and spices. It is commonly served with [[Cookbook:Tuwo Shinkafa (Nigerian Mashed Rice)|tuwo shinkafa (Nigerian Mashed Rice)]], [[Cookbook:Tuwo Masara (Nigerian Corn Fufu)|tuwo masara (Nigerian Corn Fufu)]], or [[Cookbook:Tuwon Dawa (Nigerian Sorghum Swallow)|tuwon dawa (Nigerian Sorghum Swallow)]].

== Ingredients ==
* 500 g [[Cookbook:Beef|beef]] or [[Cookbook:Goat|goat]] meat
* 1 medium [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 2–3 [[Cookbook:Dehydrated Broth|seasoning cubes]]
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]] (to taste)
* Water (as needed)
* 2 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] peeled and chunked [[Cookbook:Pumpkin|pumpkin]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] [[Cookbook:Groundnut|groundnut]] paste (optional)
* 1 tablespoon [[Cookbook:Dawadawa|fermented locust beans (''daddawa'')]]
* 2–3 tablespoons [[Cookbook:Palm Oil|palm oil]] or [[Cookbook:Peanut Oil|groundnut oil]]
* 1–2 teaspoons ground [[Cookbook:Chiles|chile pepper]] (to taste)
* 1–2 pieces [[Cookbook:Dryfish|dried or smoked fish]] (optional)
* 1 cup chopped [[Cookbook:Spinach|spinach]], [[Cookbook:Fluted Pumpkin|ugu]] leaf, or [[Cookbook:Roselle|yakuwa]] leaf (optional)

== Equipment ==
* [[Cookbook: Stock Pot|Cooking pot]]
* [[Cookbook:Knife|Knife]] and [[Cookbook:Cutting Board|cutting board]]
* [[Cookbook:Cooking Spoon|Cooking spoon]]
* [[Cookbook:Measuring Cup|Measuring cups and spoons]]
* [[Cookbook: Mixing Bowl|Mixing bowl]] (optional, for dissolving groundnut paste or soaking dried fish)

== Procedure ==
# Place the meat in a pot. Add chopped onion, seasoning cubes, salt, and enough water to cover everything. [[Cookbook:Simmering|Simmer]] until the meat is cooked through and tender to your taste—this can take a while for tough cuts of meat.
# Add pumpkin chunks to the pot. Cook until they become soft (about 10–15 minutes), then gently mash some of the pumpkin to thicken the soup.
# Add groundnut paste if using, daddawa, palm oil, chile pepper, and fish. Stir well and simmer for another 10 minutes.
# Add your leafy vegetables and cook for an additional 5 minutes.
# Add water if needed to get your desired soup thickness.
== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* ''Daddawa'' is fermented locust beans used to add deep flavor.
* Groundnut paste adds richness but can be omitted for a lighter version.
* The soup can be sweet, spicy, or both, depending on the pumpkin and chili quantity.

title: Cookbook:Mmong ikong (water leaf soup)
text:
{{recipe}}

{{Recipe summary
| Cuisine = Nigerian cuisine
| Origin = Ibibio and Efik origin
| Yield = 3-4 plates
| Servings = 3-4
| Time = 1 hour
| Difficulty = 2
}}

'''Mmong Ikong''' is a traditional Water leaf [[Cookbook:Soup|soup]] of the Efik and Ibibio people of southern Nigeria. The soup is prepared with  fresh water leafs , [[Cookbook:Seafood|seafood]], [[Cookbook:Palm Oil|palm oil]], and seasonings. It is known for its rich flavour and high nutritional value and is commonly eaten with fufu, [[Cookbook:Pounded Yam|pounded yam]], [[Cookbook:Eba (Cassava Flake Swallow)|eba]], or [[Cookbook:Semolina|semolina]].

== Ingredients ==

* chopped water leaf 
* Periwinkles (optional)
* smoked [[Cookbook:fish|fish]]
* [[Cookbook:stockfish|stockfish]], soaked and cleaned
*  grounded [[Cookbook:crayfish|crayfish]]
* 1 medium [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], chopped
* 3 tablespoons [[Cookbook:Palm Oil|palm oil]]
* 2 fresh peppers, blended
* 2 seasoning cubes
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]] to taste
* 2 cups [[Cookbook:Water|water]] or [[Cookbook:Broth and Stock|stock]]

== Equipment ==
* Cooking pot 
* [[Cookbook:Knife|Knife]]
* Bowl for washing the leaf and ingredients 
* [[Cookbook:Mortar and Pestle|Mortar and pestel]]
* Stove or cooking gas
* [[Cookbook:Spatula|Spatula]]

== Procedure ==

1. Wash and chop all the water leaf thoroughly.

2. Clean and prepare the fish, stockfish, and periwinkle

3. Cook your fish and stockfish in a separate pot.

4. Place the cooking pot on fire on medium heat.

5. Allow the pot to dry, pour in your plam oil and leave it to hot for about a minute.

6. Add chopped onions into the hot oil and strir.

7. Add in your chopped water leaf and stir, cover the pot and allow it to fry for at least 40 second.

8. Pour in your brout,add fish, stock,paper, and seasoning cubes or powder, stir and allow it to cook for a minute

9. Pour in the periwinkle and add a little water sine the water leaf already has water of it's own.

10. Cover the pot and let it cook for about 3-5 minutes 

11. Taste and adjust seasoning if necessary.

12. Remove from heat and serve hot.

== Serving ==
Mmong Ikong is traditionally served with
* [[Cookbook:fufu|fufu]]
* [[Cookbook:Pounded Yam|pounded yam]]
* [[Cookbook:eba|eba]]
* [[Cookbook:Semolina|semolina]] or other [[Cookbook:Swallow|swallow]] foods.

title: Cookbook:Molasses Cookies
text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Cookie recipes
| Difficulty = 3
| Image = [[File:Molasses-Cookies-2006March09.JPG|300px]]
}}

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of the United States|Cuisine of the United States]] | [[Cookbook:Dessert|Dessert]]

These cookies can be considered '''gingerbread cookies''', and originally were named as such. They resemble the '''molasses cookies''' made by Archway; they use relatively little [[Cookbook:Ginger|ginger]] and are thus not as spicy hot as gingerbread cookies from many other recipes. They are usually somewhat soft and not at all gooey, being halfway between crumbly and chewy. They are generally not crisp, but can be slightly crisp if thoroughly cooked. The recipe works for both drop cookies and rolled cookies, with a bit of adjustment to the amount of flour.

The known history of this recipe starts from eavesdropping on a party-line telephone during the early 1900s. The age of this recipe appears to explain many odd features. At the time, [[Cookbook:Baking Powder|baking powder]] did not exist. Thus this recipe uses [[Cookbook:Baking Soda|baking soda]], with [[Cookbook:Milk|sour milk]] (now created via [[Cookbook:Vinegar|vinegar]], so don't panic) as the acid. Ginger would have been expensive. The recipe originally called for an undefined amount of [[Cookbook:Flour|flour]] that turned out to be around 8 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] (½ [[Cookbook:Gallon|gallon]]), which would feed a family of a dozen or so. The recipe has been cut in half for the benefit of less-productive parents.

==Ingredients==

*½ [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoon]] [[Cookbook:Vinegar|vinegar]]
*½ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] [[Cookbook:Milk|milk]] (minus ½ tablespoon for the vinegar)
*½ cup [[Cookbook:Sugar|sugar]]
*½ cup (8 tablespoons) [[Cookbook:Shortening|shortening]]
*1 [[Cookbook:Egg|egg]]
*1 cup [[Cookbook:Molasses|molasses]]
*4 cups [[Cookbook:Flour|flour]]
*2 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] [[Cookbook:Baking Soda|baking soda]]
*¼ teaspoon [[Cookbook:Cinnamon|cinnamon]]
*¼ teaspoon [[Cookbook:Ginger|ginger]]
*Toppings ([[Cookbook:Walnut|walnuts]], [[Cookbook:Raisin|raisins]], etc.)

==Procedure==

[[Image:Molasses-Cookies-In-Progress-2006March09.JPG|thumb|280x280px|In progress: the drop variety,  being pressed with a sugar-covered clay stamp]]

#Grease or [[Cookbook:Parchment Paper|parchment]]-line some [[Cookbook:Cookie Sheet|cookie sheets]].
#Combine the vinegar and milk.
#Combine the baking soda, cinnamon, ginger, and 2½ cups of flour.
#[[Cookbook:Creaming|Cream]] together the sugar and shortening until well-combined, then [[Cookbook:Beating|beat]] in the molasses and egg until smooth.
#Alternately mix in the dry and milk mixtures, starting and ending with the dry mixture.
#Bit by bit, mix in more flour as needed. For drop cookies, you might not add any more. For rolled cookies produced without refrigeration, you are likely to need an extra 1½ cup for a total of 4 cups. Refrigeration can reduce this slightly.
#Chill the batter in the refrigerator for at least 1 hour.
#Form the cookies.
#*If making drop cookies, scoop some batter onto the prepared cookie sheet. Using a bit of sugar to prevent sticking, squish the cookie with a glass. Press some toppings into the top of the cookie.
#*Plop a [[Cookbook:Pint|pint]]-sized blob of batter onto a flour-dusted surface. [[Cookbook:Dusting|Dust]] the top of the dough with flour as you squish it down, then [[Cookbook:Dough#Rolling|roll it out]]. A cold marble [[Cookbook:Rolling Pin|rolling pin]] is suggested. Cut out shapes, then place them on the cookie sheet. The unused dough may be put back into the mix; note that this increases the proportion of flour.
#Bake cookies for 8–10 minutes at [[Cookbook:Oven_temperatures|375°F]].

==Notes, tips, and variations==

* Softened unsalted [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]] may be substituted for the [[Cookbook:Shortening|shortening]]. [[Cookbook:Lard|Lard]] is an even better substitute.

The following is a recipe on how to make breaded mozzarella sticks.

==Ingredients==

* ¼ [[Cookbook:Pound|pound]] fresh [[Cookbook:Mozzarella Cheese|mozzarella cheese]]
* ½ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] seasoned [[Cookbook:Bread Crumb|bread crumbs]]
* 1 large [[Cookbook:Egg|egg]]

==Procedure==
# Preheat [[Cookbook:Deep Fat Frying|deep fryer]] to 350°F (175°C).
# Slice mozzarella into sticks 1–3 cm in diameter.
# In a small bowl, [[Cookbook:Whisk|whisk]] egg.
# Fill another small bowl with bread crumbs.
# Dip 3–4 sticks at a time into the egg.
# Shake excess egg off sticks and place them in the bread crumbs. 
# Shake bowl of bread crumbs, evenly coating all sticks. Add more bread crumbs as needed.
# Place coated sticks to the side and repeat for remaining sticks.
# After all sticks have been coated, repeat the egg-dip and crumb-coat for each once more.
# Place all sticks in fryer basket and submerge in 350°F oil.
# Let sit for 30 seconds, gently rocking basket occasionally.
# Lift basket and let cool for a few seconds. If cheese is not beginning to ooze out from half the sticks, re-submerge in oil for another 10–15 seconds, gently shaking the basket.  Repeat until the cheese is just starting to ooze out.
# Dump onto [[Cookbook:Paper Towel|paper towel]] and pat off excess oil gently.
# Serve hot.

'''Moin moin''', also called '''''moimoi''''' or '''''moyin moyin''''', is a traditional West African (particularly Nigerian) dish based on black-eyed peas or other [[Cookbook:Legumes|beans]]. It is usually conical or cylindrical in shape, depending on the type of mould used. Some use small baking tins as the mould, while others use light transparent nylon bags. Traditionally, however, the moin-moin is wrapped in leaves of the Yoruba soft cane (''Thaumatococcus daniellii''). The leaves give the dish a sweetish aftertaste.
==Ingredients==
* About 2 [[Cookbook:Units of measurement#Nigeria|milk tins]] of [[Cookbook:Black-eyed Pea|black-eyed peas]], or other [[Cookbook:Legumes|beans]]
* [[Cookbook:water|Water]]
* [[Cookbook:Bell Pepper|Bell peppers]], [[Cookbook:Dice|diced]]
* [[Cookbook:Scotch Bonnet Chile|Scotch bonnet Chile peppers]], diced 
* [[Cookbook:Onion|Onion]], diced 
* About 2–3 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] [[Cookbook:Palm Oil|palm]] or [[Cookbook:Vegetable oil|vegetable oil]]
* [[Cookbook:salt|Salt]] to taste
* [[Cookbook:Bouillon Cube|Seasoning cubes]] to taste
* [[Cookbook:Hard Boiled Eggs|Hard-boiled eggs]] (optional), cut in quarters
* Dried or fresh [[Cookbook:fish|fish]] (optional)
* [[Cookbook:Beef|Beef]] (optional), in chunks or [[Cookbook:Mince|minced]]
* [[Cookbook:Liver|Liver]] (optional)

== Equipment ==
*[[Cookbook:Oven|Oven]]

*[[Cookbook: Coffee|Grinding]] machine

*[[Cookbook:Pots and Pans|Pot]]

*[[Cookbook: Cooking Spoon|Spoon]]

*[[Cookbook: Mixing Bowl|Bowl]]

==Procedure==
Traditionally, moin moin is [[Cookbook:Steaming|steamed]] rather than [[Cookbook:Baking|baked]]. Steaming is the most common method used to cook moin moin and is considered the traditional way of preparing the dish. However, some people have adapted the recipe and started baking moin moin instead of steaming it. Baking moin moin gives it a slightly different texture and flavour compared to steaming. Baking can make the moin moin denser and drier than the steamed version. Both methods are covered below. 

===Steamed===
# Place the beans in a large container. Cover them with water, and soak for about 1 hour.
# [[Cookbook:Puréeing|Blend]] all the peppers with the onion to make a smooth paste.
# Prepare [[Cookbook:Aluminium Foil|foil]] or empty cans as molds for cooking.
#* If using empty cans, make sure their interior is clean, and lightly greased.
#* If using foil:
#*#Tear off about 1 foot (30 cm) of the foil.
#*#Fold the foil in half.
#*#One of the edges is closed and fine. For two of the other edges, roll them a few times over to make sure they will take the weight of the mixture (at least an inch-worth of rolling).
#*#When you are done, the foil will look like rectangles with only one edge open.
# Rub the beans between your hands to peel the skin off. The skin should float to the top of the container. Keep doing this until you have most of the skin off the beans.
# Grind the beans into a smooth, finely-ground, mostly-liquid paste.
# Add blended mix of scotch bonnet peppers, bell peppers and onions, a few teaspoons of oil, a little salt, and the optional ingredients as desired.
# Transfer the mixture into the intended mould:
#* If using cans, simply pour some of the batter into the cans, making sure you leave enough room for the moin moin to expand.
#* If using foil, pour some of the batter into the foil, and then close up the last edge of the foil by rolling it securely.
#* If using the leaves, wrap the leaves into an open cone. Fold the bottom of the cone to prevent the mix from leaking out. Place some of the mixture to fill half the cone. Roll the top of the cone and fold it. Place the cone in such a way as to keep the folded portion flat against the cooking surface, which should also be lined with the leaves.
# Bring water to [[Cookbook:Boil|boil]] in a large pot. The water should at least cover the bottom of the pot. Less water is needed if you use the leaves. Add the filled moin moin molds. 
# Leave the moin moin to [[Cookbook:Steaming|steam]] for at least 30 minutes until it solidifies.
# Remove them from the cans or the foil before serving.
# Serve with rice, meat, custard, pap or other side dishes as desired.

===Baking===
#Grind the peeled beans alongside the pepper and onion to give a smooth paste.
#Add grounded Maggi, salt, and vegetable oil to the paste, and stir with a wooden spoon to make the ingredients uniform.
#Preheat [[Cookbook:Oven|oven]] to 200°C (390°F).
#Rub vegetable oil in the muffin cups and pour the moi moi mixture inside.
#Fold aluminum foil to the sides of the up to prevent the moi moi from drying up.
#Pour water in an oven tray and place the muffin cups in the tray
#Bake for 45 minutes, replenishing the water as necessary to prevent it from drying up.
#Leave to cool down and remove from oven when done.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* Some people recommend lightly grinding the beans before soaking them to make it easier to remove the skin.
* Some variants of this dish call for minimal or no removal of the beans' skins. The resulting moin moin is thicker than usual, and somewhat harder to digest.

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Sandwiches|Sandwiches]]

A '''Monte Cristo sandwich''' is a [[Cookbook:Sandwiches|sandwich]] composed of ham, chicken, and Swiss cheese enclosed in bread that is dipped in beaten egg and fried until golden brown. <ref>Encyclopedia of American Food and Drink, John F. Mariani [Lebhar-Friedman:New York] 1999 (p. 209)</ref>

==Ingredients==
* [[Cookbook:Butter|Butter]]
* 3 slices of white [[Cookbook:bread|bread]]

* Sliced cooked [[Cookbook:chicken|chicken]]
* Thinly-sliced [[Cookbook:Emmental Cheese|Emmental cheese]]
* [[Cookbook:egg|Egg]] [[Cookbook:batter|batter]]

==Procedure==

# Butter the first slice of bread and cover with ham and chicken.
# Butter the middle slice on both sides, place on meat, and cover with cheese.
# Butter the third slice and place, butter down, over cheese.
# Trim crusts, then cut sandwich in two and secure with [[Cookbook:Skewer|toothpicks]]
# Dip in light egg batter, and [[Cookbook:Frying|fry]] in butter on all sides until golden brown.
# Remove toothpicks and serve with currant jelly, strawberry jam, or cranberry sauce.<ref>The Brown Derby Cookbook [Doubleday & Company:Garden City NY] 1949 (p. 183)</ref>

{{recipe}}

A Monte Cristo sandwich is a sort of savory French toast sandwich. This recipe combines the traditional sandwich with the hamburger.

== Ingredients ==
* 1 [[Cookbook:Pound|pound]] 80/20 ground [[Cookbook:Beef#Chuck|chuck]]
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]]
* Freshly-ground [[Cookbook:Pepper|black pepper]]
* [[Cookbook:Olive Oil|Olive oil]]

* Few shots of hot sauce
* 1 [[Cookbook:Egg|egg]], beaten
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] [[Cookbook:Heavy Cream|heavy cream]]
* 4 slices [[Cookbook:Cheese|cheese]]
* Nonstick [[Cookbook:Cooking Spray|cooking spray]]

== Procedure ==
#Preheat [[Cookbook:Oven|oven]] to 200°F.
#Combine the egg, hot sauce, and cream in a [[Cookbook:Pie and Tart Pans|pie plate]]. Dip cut sides of buns into egg mixture. Move to a [[Cookbook:Cooling Rack|cooling rack]] and let sit 10 minutes.
#Heat a medium [[Cookbook:Non-stick|nonstick]] [[Cookbook:Frying Pan|skillet]] over medium heat. Grease with cooking spray.
#Add buns, one at a time, and cook until browned on cut side. Move to a clean plate and repeat until all buns have been cooked. Keep warm in the oven.
#Form beef into 4 equal patties. [[Cookbook:Brush|Brush]] both sides with olive oil and sprinkle both sides liberally with salt and freshly ground black pepper.
#Heat about 28 charcoal briquets in a large chimney starter. Once hot, disperse evenly around the bottom of a [[Cookbook:Grill|grill]] and reapply grate. Add patties and cook, turning often, until internal temperature reaches 145°F for medium rare, 160°F for medium, and 170°F for toast.
#Remove to a plate, top with cheese, and cover with [[Cookbook:Aluminium Foil|aluminum foil]]. Let rest 3 minutes.
#Place a patty on the bottom half of each bun. Top with upper half and serve warm.

==Ingredients==

=== Marinade ===

* 1 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] [[Cookbook:Ginger|ginger]] paste

* 2 medium sized [[Cookbook:Onion|onions]], chopped

* 3–5 whole [[Cookbook:Clove|cloves]]
* 1 medium [[Cookbook:Cinnamon|cinnamon]] stick

* 1–2 tbsp [[Cookbook:Ghee|ghee]] or [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]]
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]], according to taste

=== Serving ===
* 2 tbsp [[Cookbook:Coconut Cream|coconut cream]]/crushed coconut
* ½ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] single [[Cookbook:Cream|cream]]
* 4–6 threads [[Cookbook:Saffron|saffron]]
* A few drops [[Cookbook:Rosewater|rosewater]] (optional)
* 1 tbsp toasted flakes of [[Cookbook:Almond|almonds]] for decoration (optional)

==Procedure==

# Combine the chicken with all the marinade ingredients, cover the bowl with [[Cookbook:Plastic Wrap|cling film]], and leave in the fridge to [[Cookbook:Marinating|marinate]] for 1–3 hours.
#[[Cookbook:Frying|Fry]] the onions in ghee until it starts to turn brown but still soft. Do not fry to crispiness. Take out the onion with slotted spoon and set aside.
#Add the marinated chicken to the hot ghee and cook over medium heat.
#Dry toast the whole spices in a hot [[Cookbook:Frying Pan|frying pan]] for 1 minute until aromatic.
#Add the whole spices and black pepper to the chicken.
#Stir occasionally and cook covered.
#When water starts to separate from the chicken, add coconut cream, salt and sugar.
#Add boiling water if chicken starts to dry up before its cooked.
#Warm the single cream in microwave and add saffron to it.
#Stir in cream when almost cooked.
#Remove from the heat, and serve with fried onions, rose water, and almonds.

==Notes, tips, and variations==
* Serve with warm pilaf rice.
* Korma, being a mild dish, can be a good introduction to South Asian cuisines, especially for those who like to avoid too spicy or too hot dishes.
* Ethnic ingredient shops often sell premade fried onion packs.

=== Curry ===

* 8 [[Cookbook:Almond|almonds]]
* 10 [[Cookbook:Cashew|cashews]] or 1 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] [[Cookbook:Poppy Seed|poppy seeds]]

== Procedure ==

=== Chicken ===

# Cut chicken into bite-sized pieces and wash well.
# [[Cookbook:Marinating|Marinate]] chicken with remaining ingredients for 1–4 hours.

=== Spice blend ===

# Dry [[Cookbook:Roasting|roast]] all the ingredients until light brown and aromatic.

=== Curry ===

# Soak almonds and cashews in water for 10–15 minutes. Peel almonds.

# Add water, and cook for 3–4 minutes over medium heat.
# Mix in the nut paste, mint, and salt. Cook until gravy becomes thick and oil starts to float.
# Remove from the heat, and stir in the coriander leaves.

{{recipe summary

'''Mohingha''' is a traditional Burmese dish made of colored [[Cookbook:Soup|soup]] with rice vermicelli. Here is a modern-day recipe. It is recommended that you top your mohingha with [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]] slices and Naga viper [[Cookbook:Chiles|peppers]]; however, the use of [[Cookbook:Tabasco Sauce|Tabasco]] habanero [[Cookbook:Hot Sauce|Pepper sauce]], fish fingers, and [[Cookbook:Ginger|ginger]] is also acceptable.
[[File:Mohinga.jpg|alt=Mohingha soup powder|thumb|Mohingha soup powder]]

==Ingredients==
*5 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] [[Cookbook:Sunflower Oil|sunflower oil]]
*10 [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]] cloves
*30 [[Cookbook:Milliliter|ml]] [[Cookbook:Lemonade|lemonade]]
*70 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] Mohingha soup powder
*⅞ [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] [[Cookbook:Boiling|boiling]] water
*100 g [[Cookbook:Jalapeño|jalapeno peppers]], [[Cookbook:Dice|diced]]
*2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] [[Cookbook:Ketchup|ketchup]]
*60 g instant rice [[Cookbook:Vermicelli|vermicelli]]

==Instructions==
#In a large bowl, mix sunflower oil, garlic cloves, soup powder, and lemonade for 3 minutes.
#In a small bowl, mix boiling water, diced jalapeño peppers, and ketchup for 5 minutes.
#Combine both mixtures, and continue mixing for 2 ½ minutes.
#Add rice vermicelli to the bowl; cover it and wait for 10 minutes.
#Top it with toppings as desired.

title: Cookbook:Mofletta (Maghrebi Pancake)
text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Flatbread recipes
| Difficulty = 3
}}

{{Recipe}}

'''Mofletta''' is a thin, [[Cookbook:Crêpe|crepe-like]] pancake made by communities in North Africa, and made popular in Israel.

== Ingredients ==
* 1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] dry [[cookbook:yeast|yeast]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Pinch|pinch]] of [[cookbook:sugar|sugar]]
* ½ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] warm water
* 250 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] [[cookbook:flour|wheat flour]]
* ½ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] [[cookbook:salt|sea salt]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] of [[cookbook:olive oil|olive oil]], plus a little extra for pan-frying
* [[cookbook:butter|Butter]]
* [[cookbook:honey|Honey]]

== Procedure ==
# Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the water. Let rest in a warm place for 10–15 minutes.
# Combine flour, salt, and 1 tablespoon of oil in a bowl. Stir in the yeast mixture to make a [[Cookbook:Dough|dough]].
# [[Cookbook:Kneading|Knead]] the dough on a flat, flour-dusted surface until smooth and elastic.
# Return dough to the bowl and pour the remaining tablespoon of oil onto it, rolling the dough in the bowl until it becomes oiled.
# Cover the dough with a tea towel and leave in a warm place until it rises.
# Divide the dough into smaller equal portions, and begin to [[Cookbook:Dough#Rolling|roll]] the rounded portions out on an oiled work-surface, making them as thin as possible.
# Heat a [[Cookbook:Frying Pan|frying pan]] over medium heat, and grease the bottom with a little oil.
# [[Cookbook:Frying|Fry]] the rolled-out dough portions one at a time until they are lightly browned on one side. Flip over and cook until browned on the second side.
# Keep the finished mofletta in a stack, covered with a cloth to retain heat and moisture.
# Serve with butter and honey.

== Ingredients ==
* 3 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|Tbsp]] [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]]

* ¼ cup thinly-sliced [[Cookbook:Green Onion|green onion]] tops
* ½ Tbsp dried [[Cookbook:Parsley|parsley]]
* ¼ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] [[Cookbook:Nutmeg|nutmeg]]
* ¼ tsp [[Cookbook:Pepper|pepper]]
* 1 tsp [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
* ½ cup dry white [[Cookbook:Wine|wine]]
* 2 cups [[Cookbook:Whipping Cream|whipping cream]]
* ½ tsp Dijon [[Cookbook:Mustard|mustard]]

== Procedure ==

# In a 12-inch [[Cookbook:Non-stick|non-stick]] [[Cookbook:Skillet|skillet]], heat the butter over medium-high heat until foaming.
# Add the morels and [[Cookbook:Sautéing|sauté]], stirring occasionally, for 15–20 minutes until slightly crispy.
# Add the onion tops, parsley, nutmeg, pepper, and salt and cook for a few minutes
# Turn up the heat, add wine, and reduce to almost a glaze
# Turn heat to medium and add the cream and mustard. Reduce slightly over slow [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]] until thickened—about 10–12 minutes.
# Serve.
== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* To make this a really grand dish, add 20–24 nice-sized boiled shrimp to the sauce before serving.

title: Cookbook:Molokhia (Egyptian Jute Mallow Soup)
text:
__NOTOC__
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Soup recipes
| Time = 60-90 minutes
| Difficulty = 2
| Image = [[File:Molokhia.jpg|300px]]
}}{{Recipe}}

'''Molokhia''' is a popular Egyptian [[Cookbook:Soup|soup]] made from the leaves of the jute mallow plant. It is a comforting and flavorful dish that is often enjoyed with rice or bread. Molokhia has a unique texture and a distinct earthy taste, making it a beloved staple in Egyptian cuisine.

== Ingredients ==
* 2 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] fresh or frozen [[Cookbook:Jute|jute mallow]] (molokhia) leaves
* 4 cups vegetable or [[Cookbook:Chicken|chicken]] [[Cookbook:Broth|broth]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] [[Cookbook:olive oil|olive oil]]
* 1 large [[Cookbook:onion|onion]], finely [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 3 cloves [[Cookbook:garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Mince|minced]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] ground [[Cookbook:cumin|cumin]]
* [[Cookbook:salt|Salt]] to taste
* [[Cookbook:black pepper|Black pepper]] to taste
* Juice of 1 [[Cookbook:lemon|lemon]] (optional)
* Cooked [[Cookbook:rice|rice]] or [[Cookbook:bread|bread]] for serving

== Equipment ==
* [[Cookbook:Saucepan|Saucepan]]
* Wooden spoon or [[Cookbook:Spatula|spatula]]
* [[Cookbook:Knife|Knife]]
* [[Cookbook:Cutting Board|Cutting board]]
* Serving bowl or plate

== Procedure ==
# If using fresh molokhia leaves, remove any tough stems and wash the leaves thoroughly. If using frozen molokhia, thaw it according to the package instructions.
# In a saucepan, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the finely chopped onion and minced garlic. [[Cookbook:Sautéing|Sauté]] until the onion becomes translucent and the garlic becomes fragrant.
# Add the fresh or thawed molokhia leaves to the saucepan and stir well to combine with the onion and garlic mixture.
# Pour in the vegetable or chicken broth, ensuring that the molokhia leaves are fully submerged.
# Season the soup with ground cumin, salt, and black pepper to taste. Stir to incorporate the spices.
# Bring the soup to a gentle [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]], then reduce the heat to low and let it [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] for about 20–30 minutes, allowing the flavors to meld together.
# Remove the soup from the heat. Optionally, squeeze the juice of a lemon into the soup and stir well to enhance the flavors.
# Serve the molokhia hot, accompanied by cooked [[Cookbook:rice|rice]] or [[Cookbook:bread|bread]].

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* Molokhia is traditionally served with rice or bread. It can be enjoyed as a standalone soup or as part of a larger meal with additional side dishes. Some variations of molokhia include the addition of meat or poultry for added protein.

title: Cookbook:Muceere (Ugandan Pumpkin Stew)
text:
__NOTOC__{{recipe summary
| category = Ugandan recipes
| cuisine = Ugandan
| difficulty = 3
}}
{{Recipe}}

'''Muceere''' is a hearty and flavorful dish that celebrates the natural sweetness and richness of pumpkin. This traditional stew is made with tender chunks of pumpkin cooked in a flavorful sauce, making it a comforting and nutritious meal.

== Ingredients ==
* 2 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] [[Cookbook:Pumpkin|pumpkin]], peeled and [[Cookbook:Cube|cubed]]
* 1 cup [[Cookbook:Coconut Milk|coconut milk]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], finely [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 2 cloves of [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Mince|minced]]
* 1 red [[Cookbook:Bell Pepper|bell pepper]], [[Cookbook:Dice|diced]]
* 1 green bell pepper, diced
* 1 [[Cookbook:Tomato|tomato]], chopped
* 1 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoon]] [[Cookbook:Vegetable Oil|vegetable oil]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] [[Cookbook:Curry|curry powder]]
* 1 teaspoon [[Cookbook:Cumin|ground cumin]]
* 1 teaspoon [[Cookbook:Coriander|ground coriander]]
* ½ teaspoon [[Cookbook:Turmeric|ground turmeric]]
* ½ teaspoon [[Cookbook:Paprika|ground paprika]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Pinch|pinch]] of [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
* 1 pinch of [[Cookbook:Pepper|ground black pepper]]
* Fresh [[Cookbook:Cilantro|cilantro]] or [[Cookbook:Parsley|parsley]], chopped (for [[Cookbook:Garnish|garnish]])

== Equipment ==
* [[Cookbook:Pot and Pans|Pot]]
* [[Cookbook:Knife|Knife]]
* [[Cookbook:Cutting Board|Cutting board]]
* Spoon

== Procedure ==
# In a pot, heat the vegetable oil over medium heat.
# Add the finely chopped onion and minced garlic to the hot oil. [[Cookbook:Sautéing|Sauté]] until the onions become translucent and aromatic.
# Toss in the diced red and green bell peppers, and the chopped tomato. Cook for a few minutes until the vegetables soften and release their flavors.
# Add the curry powder, ground cumin, ground coriander, ground turmeric, and ground paprika to the pot. Stir well to coat the vegetables with the spices.
# Carefully pour in the coconut milk, and stir the mixture until the spices are well combined with the coconut milk.
# Add the cubed pumpkin to the pot, and gently mix it with the coconut milk and spice mixture.
# Season the stew with a pinch of salt and ground black pepper, to taste.
# Cover the pot and let the stew [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] over low heat for about 15–20 minutes, or until the pumpkin becomes tender and fully cooked. Stir occasionally to prevent the stew from sticking to the bottom of the pot.
# Once the pumpkin is soft and the flavors have melded together, remove the pot from the heat.
# Serve hot, [[Cookbook:Garnish|garnished]] with freshly chopped cilantro or parsley for added freshness and color.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* You can add other vegetables like [[Cookbook:Carrot|carrots]] or [[Cookbook:Green Bean|green beans]] to the stew for added texture and flavor.
* For a creamier version of muceere, you can use coconut cream instead of coconut milk. The coconut milk adds a creamy and indulgent touch.
* Adjust the level of spiciness by adding more or less ground paprika or chili flakes, depending on your preference.
* Muceere can be enjoyed as a main dish, served with rice or bread, or as a side dish to complement other Ugandan meals.
* Muceere is rich in vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber from the pumpkin and vegetables.

title: Cookbook:Muboora (Zimbabwean Pumpkin Leaves Stew)
text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Pumpkin recipes
| Difficulty = 3
}}

{{Recipe}}

'''Muboora''' is a popular Zimbabwean pumpkin leaf stew.

== Ingredients ==

* 1 bunch of fresh [[Cookbook:Pumpkin|pumpkin]] leaves (muboora)
* 1 medium-sized [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], finely [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 2–3 cloves of [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Mince|minced]]
* 2–3 ripe [[Cookbook:Tomato|tomatoes]], chopped
* 1 cup [[Cookbook:Peanut Butter|peanut butter]]
* 2–3 tablespoons [[Cookbook:Vegetable oil|vegetable oil]]
* 1 teaspoon [[Cookbook:Curry Powder|curry powder]] (optional)
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]] to taste
* [[Cookbook:Pepper|Pepper]] to taste
* Water for cooking

== Equipment ==

* Large pot or [[Cookbook:Saucepan|saucepan]]
* Wooden spoon
* [[Cookbook:Knife|Knife]]
* [[Cookbook:Cutting Board|Cutting board]]

== Procedure ==

# Wash the pumpkin leaves thoroughly and remove any tough stems or veins. [[Cookbook:Chopping|Chop]] the leaves into small pieces and set them aside.
# Heat the vegetable oil in the large pot over medium heat. Add the onions and garlic. [[Cookbook:Sautéing|Sauté]] until they become translucent and fragrant.
# Add the tomatoes and curry powder to the pot. Cook until the tomatoes break down and form a thick sauce, stirring occasionally.
# Reduce the heat to low. Gradually spoon in the peanut butter, stirring continuously. Continue stirring until the peanut butter is well blended with the tomato sauce. This should create a creamy, thick mixture.
# Start adding the chopped pumpkin leaves to the pot in batches. Stir and allow each batch to wilt and mix with the sauce before adding more. Continue this process until all the pumpkin leaves are in the pot.
# Pour in enough water to cover the mixture, making it into a stew-like consistency. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Stir everything together, ensuring the leaves are submerged.
# Cover the pot and let the muboora [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] on low heat for about 20–30 minutes. Stir occasionally and check for desired tenderness of the pumpkin leaves. Add more water if necessary to maintain the desired consistency.
# Once the pumpkin leaves are tender and the flavors are well blended, your muboora is ready to be served.

text:

'''Dough:''' 1.5 hours
'''Filling:''' 30–45 minutes | Difficulty = 3 }} {{Recipe}} This recipe for mushroom bao buns is adapted from one by Simon Rimmer.{{Citation |title=Mushroom Bao Buns {{!}} The perfect Friday meal! Treat yourself to @rimmersimon’s delicious Mushroom Bao Buns✨ Made in the @samsunguk kitchen😋 Serves 4-6 Prep time 20 mins +... {{!}} By Sunday Brunch {{!}} Facebook |url=https://www.facebook.com/SundayBrunchC4/videos/559041063134009/ |access-date=2024-11-24 |language=en}} == Ingredients == === Buns === * 500 g [[Cookbook:All-purpose flour|all-purpose flour]] * 50 g [[Cookbook:Sugar|sugar]] * 5 g [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]] * 5 g [[Cookbook:Baking Powder|baking powder]] * 5 g instant [[Cookbook:Yeast|yeast]] * 150 ml warm [[Cookbook:Water|water]] * 150 ml full-fat [[Cookbook:Milk|milk]] === Filling === * [[Cookbook:Vegetable Oil|Vegetable oil]] * 500 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] oyster [[Cookbook:Mushroom|mushrooms]], shredded * 10 ml [[Cookbook:Sesame Oil|sesame oil]] * 1 [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], [[Cookbook:Slicing|sliced]] thin * 25 mm piece fresh [[Cookbook:Ginger|ginger]], peeled and [[Cookbook:Grating|grated]] * 2 cloves [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Grating|grated]] * 50 ml rice wine [[Cookbook:Vinegar|vinegar]] * 100 ml dark [[Cookbook:Soy Sauce|soy sauce]] * 100 ml vegetable [[Cookbook:Broth and Stock|stock]] * 125 ml [[Cookbook:Maple Syrup|maple syrup]] * 5 g [[Cookbook:Chile Flakes|chile flakes]] === Serving === * [[Cookbook:Sesame Seed|Sesame seeds]] * Chopped [[Cookbook:Peanut|peanuts]] * [[Cookbook:Green Onion|Scallion]], sliced thin * Fresh red [[Cookbook:Chile|chile]], sliced thin == Procedure == === Buns === # Combine the flour, sugar, salt, baking powder, and yeast in a bowl. # Add the water and milk. Mix until you get a sticky [[Cookbook:Dough|dough]]. # Turn the dough out onto a work surface, and knead well for 10 minutes. The dough should no longer be very sticky once you have finished. # Transfer the dough back to a bowl, and cover with [[Cookbook:Plastic Wrap|plastic wrap]] or a damp towel. Let rest in a warm place for 1 hour or until doubled in size. # Gently deflate the dough, and transfer it to your work surface. # Roll the dough into an even sausage shape, and cut into 15 equal pieces. # Roll each piece into a ball, then flatten and roll with a [[Cookbook:Rolling Pin|rolling pin]] into an oval. The oval should not be too much longer than it is wide. # Brush the ovals with oil, then fold each in half with the oil on the inside. It should look like a taco shell or a purse. Don't pinch the edges together. # Cover the buns with greased plastic wrap, and let rest for 20 minutes. # Bring a few inches of water to a boil in a [[Cookbook:Steamer|steamer]]. Place the buns in the basket, and steam for 20 minutes. # Remove from the steamer. === Filling === # Heat a [[Cookbook:Frying Pan|skillet]] over medium heat, and add 2–3 tablespoons of vegetable oil. # Add the onions to the pan, and stir to coat with the oil. # Cover the pan, and turn the heat down to medium-low. Let the onions cook, stirring occasionally. As they cook, they should wilt and start to soften. Keep stirring every couple minutes to distribute the browning that accumulates at the bottom of the skillet and prevent burning. # Once the onions are a light golden color (it will take a while—be patient), remove the lid and continue cooking until deeply browned to your liking. Note that the more browned they get, the greater the risk of sticking and burning to the pan—pay attention near the end. # Remove the caramelized onions from the heat and set aside. # Heat a skillet over medium heat, then add 15 ml (1 tbsp) vegetable oil. # Add the mushrooms, and fry over medium heat for 3–4 minutes until softened. # Stir in the sesame oil, caramelized onions, ginger, garlic, vinegar, soy sauce, stock, maple syrup, and chile flakes. Cook for another 5–6 minutes until everything is soft and fragrant. # Remove the filling from the heat. === Serving === # Gently open up the buns. # Spoon some of the filling into the buns. # Garnish the filling with sesame seeds, chopped peanuts, scallion, and red chile. {{Recipe}}

'''Modeling chocolate''' is a paste made of [[Cookbook:chocolate|chocolate]] mixed with syrup. It has a consistency similar to [[Cookbook:dough|dough]] or [[Cookbook:fondant|fondant]], ideal for cake decorating. It resembles chocolate in taste, albeit with a slightly softer texture. The ratio of syrup varies depending on the amount of cocoa solids in chocolate.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-03-08 |title=Modelling chocolate |url=https://www.cocoaandheart.co.uk/modelling-chocolate/ |access-date=2024-12-18 |website=Cocoa & Heart |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Ingredients ==
* 450 [[Cookbook:g|g]] (1 [[Cookbook:lb|lb]]) [[Cookbook:chocolate|chocolate]]
* [[Cookbook:Glucose|Glucose]], [[Cookbook:Corn Syrup|corn]], or [[Cookbook:Golden Syrup|golden syrup]] as indicated by the below table, plus more as needed
{| class="wikitable"
! Type of chocolate !! Chocolate-to-syrup ratio !! Syrup amount
|-
| White chocolate || 4:1 || ⅓ cup (110 g)
|-
| Milk chocolate || 3:1 || ½ cup (150 g)
|-

|-

title: Cookbook:Mtori (Tanzanian stew)
text:
__NOTOC__{{Recipe summary
| Category = Tanzania recipes

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:African cuisines|African cuisines]] | [[Cookbook:Vegetarian_cuisine|Vegetarian Cuisine]] | [[Cookbook:Vegan_cuisine|Vegan Cuisine]]

'''Mtori''' is a traditional Tanzanian [[Cookbook:stew|stew]] made from green [[Cookbook:banana|bananas]] (plantains) and [[Cookbook:meat|meat]], usually [[Cookbook:beef|beef]]. It originated among the Chagga people of the Kilimanjaro region in northern Tanzania and has become popular throughout the country. The dish is known for its creamy texture and nourishing qualities. Mtori is commonly served for breakfast, lunch, or dinner and is especially valued as a comforting and energy-rich meal.

== Ingredients ==

* 1 kg beef with [[Cookbook:bone|bones]]
* 6–8 green cooking [[Cookbook:banana|bananas]] (plantains), peeled and sliced
* 1 large [[Cookbook:onion|onion]], chopped
* 1 [[Cookbook:carrot|carrot]], diced
* 1 green bell [[Cookbook:pepper|pepper]], chopped
* 1 [[Cookbook:potato|potato]], peeled and cubed (optional)
* 1 tbsp grated fresh [[Cookbook:ginger|ginger]]
* 2 cloves [[Cookbook:garlic|garlic]], minced
* 2 tbsp [[Cookbook:butter|butter]] or [[Cookbook:margarine|margarine]]
* 6 cups water or beef stock
* Salt, to taste
* [[Cookbook:black pepper |Black pepper]], to taste
* Fresh [[Cookbook:coriander|coriander]] (cilantro), chopped, for garnish
* [[Cookbook:Lime|Lime]] wedges, for serving (optional)

== Procedure ==

# Place the beef and water in a large pot.
# Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer until the meat is tender, about 1–1½ hours.
# Remove the meat from the stock and set aside.
# Add the bananas, onion, carrot, bell pepper, and potato to the stock.
# Cook until the bananas become very soft.
# Return the cooked meat to the pot.
# Add the ginger, garlic, salt, and black pepper.
# Simmer for 10 minutes.
# Mash the bananas using a wooden spoon or potato masher until a thick, creamy consistency is achieved.
# Stir in the butter or margarine.
# Adjust seasoning to taste.
# Simmer for another 5 minutes.
# Garnish with fresh coriander and serve hot.

== Serving ==

Mtori is traditionally served with:

* [[Cookbook:Chapati]]
* [[Cookbook:Ugali]]
* Fresh chili sauce
* Lime wedges
* Roasted meat

== Variations ==

* Chicken mtori
* Goat meat mtori
* Coconut milk mtori
* Vegetarian mtori
* Spicy mtori with chili peppers

== Tips ==

* Use green cooking bananas rather than ripe bananas for an authentic flavor.
* Beef with bones produces a richer and more flavorful stock.
* Mash the bananas while still hot for a smoother texture.
* Add coconut milk near the end of cooking for a creamier variation.
* Freshly squeezed lime juice enhances the flavor when serving.
* The stew should be thick but still easy to spoon.

== Notes ==

* Mtori originated in the Kilimanjaro region among the Chagga people.
* A traditional wooden mashing stick is often used to prepare the dish.
* It is commonly prepared using green bananas and beef cooked into a thick stew.
* Mtori is considered a hearty and nutritious meal throughout Tanzania.

'''Msemmen''' (Arabic: مسمن, romanized: musamman or msamman), also known as rghaif (رغايف), is a traditional layered flatbread from the Maghreb region of North Africa, particularly popular in Algeria and Morocco. It is prepared by folding dough into square-shaped [[Cookbook:pancake|pancakes]] containing several thin layers, which are then cooked on a [[Cookbook:griddle|griddle]]. Msemmen is commonly enjoyed with [[Cookbook:honey|honey]], mint tea, or [[Cookbook:coffee|coffee]] for breakfast. Some varieties are filled with ingredients such as preserved meat (khlea), onions, and tomatoes. The smaller forms of msemmen are believed to have originated among the Berber people.

== Ingredients ==
* 2 cups all-purpose [[Cookbook:flour|flour]]
* 1 cup fine [[Cookbook:semolina|semolina]]
* 1 teaspoon salt
* 1 teaspoon sugar
* 1 teaspoon instant yeast
* 1¼ cups warm water
* ¼ cup [[Cookbook:Vegetable Oil|vegetable oil]]
* ¼ cup melted butter

== Procedure ==
# Mix the flour, semolina, salt, sugar, and yeast in a bowl.
# Gradually add warm water and knead until a smooth dough forms.
# Divide the dough into small balls and let rest for 30 minutes.
# Flatten each ball into a thin sheet.
# Brush with oil and butter, then fold into a square.
# Let the folded squares rest for 15 minutes.
# Flatten gently and cook on a hot griddle until golden brown on both sides.
# Serve warm with honey, jam, tea, or savory accompaniments.

== Notes ==
* M'semen (also spelled Msemen or Msemmen) is a traditional layered flatbread from the Maghreb, especially Morocco and Algeria.
* It is commonly served for breakfast or tea time.

== Variations ==
* Stuffed M'semen with onions and tomatoes.
* Sweet M'semen served with honey and butter.
* Mlewi, a rolled spiral variation.

'''Mukimo''' is a traditional Kenyan dish made by mashing boiled [[Cookbook:potatoes|potatoes]] with [[Cookbook:vegetable|green vegetables]] and [[Cookbook:legumes|legumes]] such as [[Cookbook:peas|peas]], [[Cookbook:maize|maize]], or [[Cookbook:beans|beans]]. It is especially associated with the Kikuyu people of central Kenya and is commonly served as an accompaniment to [[Cookbook:stews|stews]] and [[Cookbook:meat|grilled meat]].

== Ingredients ==
* 1 kg [[Cookbook:potatoes|potatoes]], peeled and chopped
* 2 cups [[Cookbook:maize|maize]] kernels (fresh or frozen)
* 1 cup green peas
* 2 cups pumpkin leaves, spinach, or kale, chopped
* 1 teaspoon salt

== Procedure ==
# Place the potatoes, maize, and peas in a large pot and cover with water.
# Bring to a boil and cook until the potatoes are tender.
# Add the chopped vegetables and continue cooking for 5–10 minutes.
# Drain excess water if necessary.
# Mash all the ingredients together until well combined.
# Season with salt to taste.
# Serve hot with beef stew, chicken stew, or grilled meat.

== Notes ==
* Mukimo is a staple dish in Kenya, particularly in the central highlands.
* Different regions use different leafy greens depending on local availability.
* Some versions include beans instead of peas.

== Variations ==

* Mukimo with pumpkin leaves
* Mukimo with cabbage
* Mukimo with spinach and sweet potatoes

{{Recipe}}

'''Mukhbaza''' is a traditional flatbread associated with the [[Cookbook:Cuisines|cuisine]] of Sudan and neighboring regions of Northeast Africa. It is made from [[Cookbook:Wheat Flour|wheat flour]], water, [[Cookbook:yeast|yeast]], and [[Cookbook:salt|salt]], producing a soft [[Cookbook:bread|bread]] that is commonly served alongside [[Cookbook:stews|stews]], [[Cookbook:meat|meat]] dishes, and [[Cookbook:vegetable|vegetable]]-based meals. Mukhbaza is an important staple food and is often prepared in homes and bakeries throughout Sudan.

== Ingredients ==

* 500 g wheat [[Cookbook:flour|flour]]
* 1 tsp salt
* 1 tsp active dry yeast
* 300 ml warm water
* 1 tbsp [[Cookbook:Vegetable Oil|vegetable oil]]

== Procedure ==

In a large bowl, combine the flour, salt, and yeast.

Gradually add the warm water while mixing to form a soft dough.

Knead the dough for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.

Cover the dough and allow it to rise in a warm place for about 1 hour, or until doubled in size.

Divide the dough into small portions and shape each into a flat round.

Heat a griddle or heavy frying pan over medium heat.

Lightly brush the surface with oil.

Cook each flatbread for 2–3 minutes on each side until lightly browned and cooked through.

Remove from heat and keep warm until serving.

== Serving ==
Mukhbaza is commonly served with:

* Meat stews
* Lentil dishes
* Vegetable sauces
* Grilled meats
* Tea or other beverages

== Variations ==

* Whole wheat flour may be used for a denser texture.
* Some versions include sesame seeds.
* The bread may be baked instead of cooked on a griddle.

== Notes ==

* The dough should remain soft for the best texture.
* Cooking times may vary depending on the thickness of the bread.
* Mukhbaza is best served fresh and warm.

* Pita Bread
* [[Cookbook:Injera]]

== Ingredients ==

# Make the dough by [[Cookbook:Kneading|kneading]] together all the ingredients and sufficient water (this will be approximately ¾ cup but some judgement is required).

# The naans should puff up a little, and be ready to remove from the oven in 4–5 minutes.
# [[Cookbook:Brush|Brush]] the naan with butter. Serve hot.

* To add an extra crispy finish, pop the baked naans under a preheated grill for 30 seconds before brushing with butter and serving.

title: Cookbook:Never Fail Pie Crust
text:
{{recipesummary|category=Pastry recipes
| Yield = 3 pie crusts|time=30 minutes|difficulty=2|
}}

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Dessert|Dessert]]

This quick pastry is a no-fail recipe made easily with ingredients usually found in most kitchens. Be sure to use cold water and keep well-wrapped until ready to use.

In contrast to [[Cookbook:Bread|bread]], pie crust and other pastries should be made in a way that minimizes the development of [[Cookbook:Gluten|gluten]]. Once the water has been added, the dough should be worked as little as possible, to minimize toughness in the finished crust.

== Ingredients ==

* 3 [[cookbook:Cup|cup]]s (700 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]]) [[Cookbook:Flour|flour]]
* 1¼ cup (300 g) [[Cookbook:Shortening|shortening]]
* 1 [[cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
* 1 [[cookbook:Egg|egg]], beaten
* ⅓ cup (80 ml) cold water
* 1 [[cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoon]] white [[cookbook:vinegar|vinegar]]

== Procedure ==

# Combine flour, shortening and salt. Cut in shortening with fork (or pastry blender) until it resembles corn meal.
# Combine water and vinegar with beaten egg. Add to flour mixture a little at a time until a soft dough forms.
# Divide dough into three discs, and use or freeze individually.
# When using, roll out onto a floured surface to desired measurements.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* When baking two pies at once, rotate the pies 180 degrees at 15 minutes and 45 minutes to ensure the crust does not burn due to its proximity to the oven walls.

title: Cookbook:New Mexico Chili Verde
text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Chili recipes
| Servings = 5–6
| Difficulty = 3
}}

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of the United States|Cuisine of the United States]] | [[Cookbook:Southwestern cuisine|Southwestern cuisine]]

'''New Mexico Chile Verde''' is the most popular version of [[cookbook:chili con carne|chili con carne]] in the U.S. state of New Mexico. While there apparently is no canonical recipe for Chile Verde (''green chile''), <!--- that I have been able to find---> all versions involve roasting fresh green chile peppers and cooking them slowly with meat (usually [[Cookbook:Pork|pork]] but also [[Cookbook:Beef|beef]], [[Cookbook:Chicken|chicken]], or [[Cookbook:Turkey|turkey]]), [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Oregano|oregano]], and [[Cookbook:Cumin|cumin]]. The consistency is usually much thinner than Texas-style chili and is sometimes listed on restaurant menus as "green chile stew". In addition to being eaten by the bowl (sometimes with [[Cookbook:Pinto Bean|pinto beans]] or diced [[Cookbook:Potato|potatoes]] added), Chili Verde often is treated as a condiment and is ladled over [[Cookbook:Burrito|burritos]], [[Cookbook:Enchilada|enchiladas]], [[Cookbook:Hamburger|hamburgers]], and [[Cookbook:Fried Eggs|fried eggs]].

The following is a representative recipe for chili verde, but there are many variations:

==Ingredients==
*2 green [[Cookbook:Bell Pepper|bell peppers]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]] (not frequently used in New Mexico)
*4 large, mild green [[Cookbook:Chili Pepper|chile peppers]]
*5 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] [[Cookbook:Water|water]]
*1 large can (16 [[Cookbook:Ounce|oz]]) stewed [[Cookbook:Tomato|tomatoes]]
*2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] [[Cookbook:Pork|pork]] [[Cookbook:Bouillon Cube|bouillon]] granules
*1 tablespoon dried [[Cookbook:Oregano|oregano]]
*1 tablespoon whole [[Cookbook:Cumin|cumin]] seeds
*1 tablespoon [[Cookbook:Coriander|coriander]]
*8 [[Cookbook:Ounce|oz]] ground [[Cookbook:Pork|pork]]
*1 large [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
*6 tablespoons [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]] or [[Cookbook:Margarine|margarine]]
*⅓ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] (240 [[Cookbook:Milliliter|ml]]) [[Cookbook:All-purpose flour|all-purpose flour]]

==Procedure==
#Combine bell peppers, chili peppers, water, tomatoes, bouillon, oregano, cumin, and coriander in a large pot. Cook over medium heat until peppers are tender.
#Meanwhile, cook pork and onion in a [[Cookbook:Skillet|skillet]] over medium heat, stirring occasionally, about ten minutes, or until pork is browned and crumbly. Drain pork and add to chile mixture. [[Cookbook:Simmer|Simmer]] for 20 minutes.
#Heat butter in the skillet over medium-low heat. Add flour. Cook, stirring frequently, until flour browns, about 2 minutes. 
#Add flour mixture to chile. Continue cooking and stirring until thickened to preference.

==Notes, tips, and variations==
*If fresh green chili peppers are not available, dried [[Cookbook:Anaheim chili|Anaheim]] chili peppers may be substituted, but the results will be substantially different.

text:
{{recipesummary|category=Soup recipes|servings=12|time=1 hour|difficulty=3
| Image = [[Image:Corba od pecuraka.jpg|300px]]
}}
{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of the United States|American cuisine]] | [[Cookbook:Vegetarian cuisine|Vegetarian Cuisine]] | [[Cookbook:Soups|Soups]]

This recipe is originally by Chef Taylor Piercefield.

==Ingredients==

* ½ [[Cookbook:Pound|pound]] (2 sticks) [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]], divided
* 1 [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] [[Cookbook:Flour|flour]], divided
* 12 cups [[Cookbook:Stock|beef stock]]
* 6 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] extra-virgin [[Cookbook:Olive Oil|olive oil]]
* 4 cups [[Cookbook:Slicing|sliced]] [[Cookbook:Portobello Mushroom|portobello mushrooms]]
* 4 cups sliced [[Cookbook:Shiitake|shiitakes]]
* 4 cups [[Cookbook:Button Mushroom|button mushrooms]], sliced if large
* ½ cup [[Cookbook:Wine|sherry]]

==Procedure==

# In a large pot over medium heat, melt one stick of the butter.
# Add ½ cup of the flour, stirring constantly, to form a [[Cookbook:Roux|roux]].
# Cook, continuing to stir constantly, until roux takes on a pale blond color, about 5 minutes.
# Slowly stir in the beef stock.
# Bring to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]], stirring frequently.
# Reduce heat to a [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]].
# In a large [[Cookbook:saucepan|saucepan]] over medium-high heat, melt the remaining stick of butter with the olive oil.
# Add the portobellos, shiitakes, and button mushrooms and [[Cookbook:Sauté|sauté]] until mushrooms are moist and tender, 5–10 minutes.
# Remove pan from heat and dust mushrooms with the remaining ½ cup of flour, [[Cookbook:Mixing#Tossing|tossing]] gently to incorporate flour.
# Combine mushrooms and beef stock in the large pot.
# Stir in the sherry.
# Cook, stirring occasionally, until flavors are melded and soup thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.
# Serve hot.

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of the United States|American cuisine]] | [[Cookbook:Seafood|Seafood]] | [[Cookbook:Soups|Soups]]

'''New England clam chowder''' is a dairy-based seafood chowder or thick soup originating in the northeastern United States. It is often thickened with a roux, and it usually contains minimal vegetables save for potatoes and onions.

==Ingredients==
* 1 [[Cookbook:Pound|pound]] canned [[Cookbook:Clam|clams]], [[Cookbook:Mince|minced]], or 12 [[Cookbook:Ounce|ounces]] frozen, thawed
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] plain white [[Cookbook:Flour|flour]]
* 1 medium [[Cookbook:Potato|potato]], [[Cookbook:Dice|diced]]
* 1 medium [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], diced
* 1 [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] [[Cookbook:Boiling|boiling]] [[Cookbook:Water|water]]
* 3 ounces salt [[Cookbook:Pork|pork]], diced
* 1½ [[Cookbook:Quart|quarts]] [[w:Fat content of milk|skimmed]] or [[cookbook:milk|whole milk]] , [[Cookbook:Scald|scalded]]
* 1 tablespoon [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]]
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]] and [[Cookbook:Pepper|pepper]] to taste

==Procedure==
# If using frozen clams, drain and reserve liquid.
# Cut hard parts away and keep them separate.
# [[Cookbook:Sautéing|Sauté]] salt pork in a heavy iron pot until brown and crisp.
# Remove pork and sauté hard part of clam and onions in hot fat until onion is light brown.
# Stir in flour, then slowly add boiling water, salt, pepper, and diced potato.
# Cover and [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] gently 10 minutes or until potato is tender.
# Add soft parts of clams and liquid.
# Just before serving, stir in scalded milk and butter.
# Heat thoroughly, but not to boiling.
# Serve piping hot with oyster or soda [[Cookbook:Hard Tack|crackers]].

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Dessert|Desserts]]

'''Nanaimo Bars''' are a layered chocolate and [[Cookbook:Custard|custard]] dessert named after the mining town, Nanaimo, British Columbia, Canada. This winning recipe was submitted by Joyce Hardcastle in 1986 when the City of Nanaimo and Harbour Park Mall had a contest to find the best Nanaimo Bar recipe. Variations of this recipe include using different nuts and/or adding flavours to the custard layer.

== Ingredients ==

=== Bottom layer ===
* ½ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] unsalted [[Cookbook:butter|butter]] (European style cultured)
* ¼ cup white granulated [[Cookbook:sugar|sugar]]
* 5 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] [[Cookbook:cocoa|cocoa]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:egg|egg]] beaten
* 1¼ cups [[Cookbook:Graham Cracker|graham wafer]] crumbs
* ½ cups finely-[[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]] [[Cookbook:almond|almonds]]
* 1 cup [[Cookbook:coconut|coconut]]

=== Middle layer ===
* ½ cup unsalted [[Cookbook:butter|butter]]
* 2 tbsp and 2 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] [[Cookbook:cream|cream]]
* 2 tbsp vanilla [[Cookbook:Custard Powder|custard powder]]
* 2 cups [[Cookbook:Powdered Sugar|icing sugar]]

=== Top layer ===
* 4 squares (4 oz) semi-sweet [[Cookbook:chocolate|chocolate]]
* 2 tbsp unsalted [[Cookbook:butter|butter]]

== Procedure ==

=== Bottom layer ===
#Melt first 3 ingredients in top of [[Cookbook:Double Boiler|double boiler]].
#Add egg and stir to cook and thicken.
#Remove from heat. Stir in crumbs, coconut, and nuts.
#Press firmly into an ungreased 8 x 8-inch [[Cookbook:Cake Pan|cake pan]].

=== Middle layer ===
#[[Cookbook:Creaming|Cream]] butter, cream, custard powder, and icing sugar together well. [[Cookbook:Beating|Beat]] until light. 
#Spread over bottom layer.

=== Top layer ===
#Melt chocolate and butter over low heat. Cool. 
#Once cool, but still liquid, pour over second layer and chill in refrigerator.
#Once set, cut into squares and serve. Enjoy.
