title: Cookbook:Sharba Libya (Libyan Soup)
text:
__NOTOC__
{{recipe summary
| category = Soup recipes
| difficulty = 3
|Time= 1 hour 30 minutes
}}
{{Recipe}}

'''Sharba Libya''' is a traditional and hearty [[Cookbook:Soup|soup]] enjoyed throughout Libya. It is made with a combination of vegetables, legumes, aromatic spices, and tender chunks of meat. It is a comforting and nourishing dish that is perfect for colder days or as a satisfying meal any time of the year.

== Ingredients ==
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] [[Cookbook:olive oil|olive oil]]
* 500 [[Cookbook:Gram|grams]] (1 [[Cookbook:Pound|lb]]) [[Cookbook:Lamb|lamb]] or [[Cookbook:Beef|beef,]] cut into small cubes
* 1 large [[Cookbook:onion|onion]], finely [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 4 cloves of [[Cookbook:garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Mince|minced]]
* 2 medium [[Cookbook:carrot|carrots]], peeled and [[Cookbook:Dice|diced]]
* 2 medium [[Cookbook:potato|potatoes]], peeled and diced
* 2 stalks of [[Cookbook:celery|celery]], diced
* 1 green [[Cookbook:Bell Pepper|bell pepper]], diced
* 1 red bell pepper, diced
* 1 [[Cookbook:zucchini|zucchini]], diced
* 1 [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] [[Cookbook: pea|green peas]] (fresh or frozen)
* 1 cup [[Cookbook:chickpea|chickpeas]], cooked or canned
* 1 cup [[Cookbook:macaroni|macaroni]] or other small [[Cookbook:Pasta|pasta]]
* 2 ripe [[Cookbook:tomato|tomatoes]], diced
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] [[Cookbook:tomato|tomato paste]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] ground [[Cookbook:cumin|cumin]]
* 1 teaspoon ground [[Cookbook:paprika|paprika]]
* ½ teaspoon ground [[Cookbook:turmeric|turmeric]]
* ½ teaspoon ground [[Cookbook:cayenne pepper|cayenne pepper]]
* ½ teaspoon ground [[Cookbook:cinnamon|cinnamon]]
* ½ teaspoon ground [[Cookbook:coriander|coriander]]
* [[Cookbook:salt|Salt]] to taste
* [[Cookbook:pepper|Pepper]], to taste
* Fresh [[Cookbook:parsley|parsley]] or [[Cookbook:cilantro|cilantro]], chopped, for [[Cookbook:Garnish|garnish]]

== Equipment ==
* Large [[Cookbook:Pots and Pans|pot]]
* Skimmer or [[Cookbook:Slotted Spoon|slotted spoon]]
* Wooden spoon or [[Cookbook:Spatula|spatula]]
* [[Cookbook:Cutting Board|Cutting board]]
* Chef's [[Cookbook:Knife|knife]]
* Measuring spoons
* Measuring cups
* Soup [[Cookbook:Ladle|ladle]]
* Serving bowls

== Procedure ==
# Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and minced garlic, and [[Cookbook:Sautéing|sauté]] until they become translucent and fragrant.
# Add the diced lamb or beef cubes to the pot and cook until browned on all sides. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking.
# Once the meat is browned, add the diced carrots, potatoes, celery, green and red bell peppers, zucchini, green peas, and chickpeas to the pot. Stir well to combine with the meat.
# Add the diced tomatoes, tomato paste, cumin, paprika, turmeric, cayenne pepper, cinnamon, coriander, salt, and pepper to the pot. Stir to coat the ingredients with the spices and tomato paste.
# Pour enough water into the pot to cover all the ingredients. Bring the soup to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]], then reduce the heat to low, cover the pot, and let it [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] for about 1 hour. This allows the flavors to meld together and the meat to become tender.
# In the meantime, cook the macaroni or small pasta according to the package instructions. Drain and set aside.
# After the soup has simmered for an hour, taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and pepper if needed.
# Add the cooked macaroni or small pasta to the soup and stir to incorporate. Let the soup simmer for another 10 minutes to allow the pasta to absorb the flavors.
# Remove the pot from the heat. Ladle into serving bowls and garnish with fresh chopped parsley or cilantro.
# Serve the soup hot with crusty bread on the side.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* Feel free to customize the vegetables used in the soup according to your preference or what's available. Other common additions include [[Cookbook:Cabbage|cabbage]], [[Cookbook:Green Bean|green beans]], or [[Cookbook:Corn|corn]].
* The soup can be made in advance and stored in the refrigerator. The flavors will deepen and the soup will thicken slightly upon chilling
* For a richer flavor, you can use bone-in meat instead of boneless. Simply remove the bones before serving.
* If the soup becomes too thick upon reheating, you can add a little water or broth to adjust the consistency.
* For a vegetarian version, omit the meat and use vegetable broth instead of water.
* Add a squeeze of fresh lemon juice to the soup just before serving for a refreshing citrus note.

title: Cookbook:Shiro (Ethiopian Spiced Chickpea or Lentil Stew)
text:
__NOTOC__
{{recipe summary
| category = Main course recipes
| difficulty = 3
}}
{{recipe}}

'''Shiro''' is a flavorful Ethiopian [[Cookbook:Stew|stew]] made with spiced chickpea or lentil flour. It is a popular vegetarian dish that is rich in protein and aromatic spices. Shiro has a thick and creamy consistency, making it perfect for scooping up with injera, the traditional Ethiopian flatbread. This delicious stew is easy to make and full of comforting flavors.
== Ingredients ==
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] [[Cookbook:olive oil|olive oil]]
* 1 large [[Cookbook:onion|onion]], finely [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 3 cloves of [[Cookbook:garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Mince|minced]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] shiro powder (chickpea or lentil flour)
* 4 cups [[Cookbook:broth|vegetable broth]] or water
* 1 tablespoon [[Cookbook:berbere|berbere spice blend]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] ground [[Cookbook:cumin|cumin]]
*½ teaspoon ground [[Cookbook:turmeric|turmeric]]
* ½ teaspoon [[Cookbook:salt|salt]], or to taste
*¼ teaspoon [[Cookbook:black pepper|black pepper]]
* Fresh [[Cookbook:parsley|parsley]] or [[Cookbook:cilantro|cilantro]], chopped, for [[Cookbook:Garnish|garnish]]

== Equipment ==
* Large [[Cookbook:Pots and Pans|pot]]
* Wooden spoon or [[Cookbook:Spatula|spatula]]
* [[Cookbook:Cutting Board|Cutting board]]
* [[Cookbook:Knife|Knife]]

== Procedure ==
# Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat.
# Add the chopped onion to the pot and [[Cookbook:Sautéing|sauté]] until translucent and slightly browned.
# Add the minced garlic to the pot and sauté for an additional minute until fragrant.
# Sprinkle the berbere spice blend, ground cumin, ground turmeric, salt, and black pepper over the onions and garlic. Stir well to coat the ingredients with the spices.
# Add the shiro powder to the pot and stir it into the onion and spice mixture.
# Gradually pour in the vegetable broth or water while continuously stirring to prevent any lumps from forming.
# Bring the mixture to a gentle [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]], then reduce the heat to low and let it [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] for about 20–25 minutes, stirring occasionally. The stew will thicken and develop a rich flavor.
# Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and pepper if needed.
# Remove the pot from the heat and let the shiro rest for a few minutes before serving.
# Garnish the shiro with fresh chopped parsley or cilantro. Serve hot with injera or bread for dipping.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* Shiro powder is available in Ethiopian or specialty grocery stores. It comes in both chickpea and lentil varieties. Choose the one you prefer or try a combination of both.
* If the shiro stew becomes too thick upon standing, you can adjust the consistency by adding a little more vegetable broth or water and stirring until desired thickness is achieved.
* For a heartier version, you can add cooked and chopped vegetables like [[Cookbook:Carrot|carrots]], [[Cookbook:Potato|potatoes]], or [[Cookbook:Spinach|spinach]] to the stew.
* Some variations of shiro include the addition of minced meat or ground beef for extra richness and flavor.
* Customize the spiciness of the shiro by adjusting the amount of berbere spice blend according to your taste preferences.

title: Cookbook:Shepherd's Pie III
text:
{{Recipesummary

{{Recipe}}

== Ingredients ==
* 100 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] minced [[Cookbook:Lamb|lamb]]
* 1 clove of [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 4 large [[Cookbook:Potato|potatoes]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Carrot|carrot]]
* Some fresh green [[Cookbook:Pea|peas]]
* Some [[Cookbook:Corn|sweetcorn]] kernels
* Mixed vegetables
* Small amount of tomato [[Cookbook:Ketchup|ketchup]]
* Beef [[Cookbook:Dehydrated Broth|stock cube]] or gravy
* 5 g [[Cookbook:Flour|flour]]
* 10 [[Cookbook:Milliliter|ml]] water
* 30 ml [[Cookbook:Milk|milk]]
* 30 g [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]] or [[Cookbook:Margarine|margarine]]
* 5 ml [[Cookbook:Olive Oil|olive oil]] or other cooking oil

== Procedure ==
# Peel and [[Cookbook:Chopping|chop]] the potatoes. [[Cookbook:Boiling|Boil]] the potatoes for 20 minutes whilst preparing the rest of the meal.

title: Cookbook:Shoofly Pie
text:
__NOTOC__ {{recipe summary | category = Pie recipes | Yield = 1 pie | servings = | Time = Active: 1 hour
Total: 2 hours | difficulty = 3 | image = [[File:Shoofly-pie-lancaster-county.jpg|300px]] | energy = | note = }} {{recipe}} '''Shoofly pie''' is a [[Cookbook:Molasses|molasses]] crumb [[Cookbook:Pie|pie]] that originated in the US in the late 19th century among the Pennsylvania Dutch communities. A strongly flavored pie, it was traditionally served cold with a cup of hot coffee as a quick breakfast for a busy farmer. This "wet-bottom" version is adapted from a recipe found in an old recipe scrapbook, which was re-published in ''The New York Times'' in both 1965 and 2022. Other versions use baking powder instead of baking soda, adjust the spices, or cook the pie until it is solid ("dry-bottom"). == Ingredients == {| class="wikitable" style="background: none;color:inherit;" !Ingredient !Count !Volume !Weight |- ! colspan="4" |Pie crust |- |Bottom [[Cookbook:Pie Crust|pie crust]] |1 ea. |– |– |- ! colspan="4" |Streusel filling |- |[[Cookbook:Butter|Butter]], cold and cubed |1 stick |½ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] |115 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] |- |[[Cookbook:All-purpose flour|All-purpose flour]] | |1½ cups |180 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] |- |[[Cookbook:Sugar|Brown sugar]], preferably dark | |½ cup |100 g |- |Ground [[Cookbook:Cinnamon|cinnamon]] | |1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] |3 g |- |Ground [[Cookbook:Nutmeg|nutmeg]] | |½ teaspoon |1 g |- ! colspan="4" |Molasses filling |- |Boiling water | |¾ cup (6 fl oz) |170 g |- |Light unsulphured [[Cookbook:Molasses|molasses]] | |¾ cup |250 g |- |[[Cookbook:Baking Soda|Baking soda]] | |½ teaspoon |3 g |} == Equipment == * Generously sized heat-proof bowl or pitcher (such as a 1-quart glass measuring pitcher) * [[Cookbook:Mixer|Mixing spoon]] * Standard-size (9-inch/23-cm) [[Cookbook:Pie and Tart Pans|pie plate]] * [[Cookbook:Parchment Paper|Parchment paper]] or a paper coffee filter * [[Cookbook:Pie Weights|Pie weights]] (see notes) * [[Cookbook:Pie Crust Shield|Pie crust shield]] or [[Cookbook:Aluminium Foil|aluminum foil]] * [[Cookbook:Oven|Oven]] == Procedure == === Par-bake pie crust === [[File:Empty_blind_baked_pie_crust.png|thumb|Single-crust pie shell, empty and parbaked (partially baked)]] # Fit your raw pie crust into the pie plate. Because the pie filling is liquid, do not [[Cookbook:Docking|dock]] (prick holes in) the dough or use a perforated pie plate. Patch any accidental holes or tears you see. Shape the [[Cookbook:Pie Crust Edges|pie crust edges]] however you would like. # Freeze the empty pie crust for 15 minutes, or refrigerate it for at least 30 minutes. # Preheat the [[Cookbook:Oven|oven]] to [[Cookbook:Oven Temperatures|375 °F (190 °C, gas mark 5, moderately hot)]]. # Line the cold pie crust with parchment paper or a paper coffee filter that is big enough to cover the entire pie, from edge to edge, when pressed down. # Fill the paper with pie weights. These will hold the parchment paper against the side of the pie crust, to keep it from melting and sliding down the edges in the oven. # [[Cookbook:Baking|Bake]] for 20–25 minutes. Remove it from the oven, and then remove the pie weights and the paper. Discard the paper. The pie weights can be stored and reused. # Turn the oven temperature up to 450 °F (230 °C, gas mark 8, hot/very hot). === Make the streusel === # Transfer the butter pieces, flour, brown sugar, and spices into a mixing bowl. # [[Cookbook:Mixing#Cutting|Cut]] or rub the ingredients together. You can do this with a [[Cookbook:Pastry Blender|pastry blender]], wooden spoon, or electric mixer. Stop before the mixture is completely blended together—you should still be able to see some small lumps of butter. # Spread at least a quarter of the raw streusel filling across the bottom of the parbaked pie crust. === Make the molasses filling === # Stir the boiling water and molasses together in the heat-proof bowl. # Working quickly, stir the baking soda into the molasses-water mixture, and then immediately pour it into the pie crust, on top of the streusel filling. # Top with the rest of the streusel filling, spreading it flat with your hand or the back of a spoon if needed. # Cover the edges of the crust with a pie crust shield or aluminum foil, so they will be less likely to overcook. # Carefully put the pie in the oven to bake. The boiling hot liquid filling will slosh when you move the pie, so move slowly. You may want to put a [[Cookbook:Baking Sheet|baking sheet]] under the pie to catch any drips. # Bake at 450 °F (230 °C, gas mark 8, hot/very hot) for 15 minutes. # Reduce the temperature to 350 °F (175 °C, gas mark 4, moderate/medium) for another 20 minutes. The pie filling should be set (i.e. it should not wiggle when you take it out of the oven), but the exact amount of doneness is a matter of personal preference. # Let cool before serving—if you don't, it will make a mess when you cut it. == Notes, tips, and variations == * If you don't have pie weights, you can use an inexpensive, dry ingredient like sugar or uncooked rice. If you use white sugar or white rice while blind-baking your pie crust, the weight can be re-used several times. Store in an ordinary airtight container at room temperature. After helping you parbake or blind-bake several pie crusts, the white sugar becomes toasted sugar, which can be used in baked goods, especially delicately flavored cakes and cookies. * Serve with coffee or tea, either by itself or accompanied by vanilla [[Cookbook:Ice Cream|ice cream]], cinnamon ice cream, or lightly sweetened [[Cookbook:Whipped Cream|whipped cream]]. While it is now usually served like any other slice of pie (with a fork and on a small plate), it is traditional to pick up a slice of shoofly pie and eat it with your hands. * Store at room temperature. It keeps well for a couple of days. * This recipe assumes American-style ingredients. Brown sugar in other countries may be too dry. If you don't have "sticky" American-style brown sugar, stir together the same amount of ordinary white sugar and 10 g of molasses to make a homemade brown sugar substitute. * The so-called "light" molasses called for here is a very dark brown syrup. The most common brands in the US are Grandma's and Brer Rabbit, but any brand of molasses will do. Sometimes "dark" or "full flavor" molasses are available; this even darker brown molasses will work, but it will produce a stronger flavor, which may not be desired. Do not use blackstrap molasses, which is too bitter, and do not use sulphured molasses, which will have a chemical flavor. If you can't get molasses, try dark corn syrup, sometimes called "Karo" after the most popular brand in the US—it will have a milder taste. If you think you would prefer a milder flavor, then substitute dark Karo for part of the molasses. * If you are measuring ingredients by volume, first lightly oil the cup you're using to measure the molasses. Then the molasses will not stick to the inside of the measuring cup as much. * This recipe can be made vegan by using a vegan butter substitute and a vegan pie crust. '''Shitha''' is a traditional spicy sauce commonly found in Arabian and Gulf cuisines, especially in countries like Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar. It is typically served as a condiment with rice dishes such as kabsa and mandi.

== Ingredients ==
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] red [[Cookbook:Chiles|chile]] powder (or fresh red chilies, blended)
* 2 medium [[Cookbook:tomato|tomatoes]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 2 [[Cookbook: clove|cloves]] [[Cookbook: garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Mince|minced]]
* 1 tablespoon [[Cookbook:Vegetable Oil|vegetable oil]]
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]] to taste
* 1 tablespoon [[Cookbook:lemon juice|lemon juice]] or [[Cookbook: Vinegar|vinegar]] (optional)

== Special equipment ==
* Small [[Cookbook:Saucepan|saucepan]] or [[Cookbook:Frying Pan|frying pan]]
* Wooden spoon or [[Cookbook:Spatula|spatula]]
* [[Cookbook:Blender|Blender]] (optional, for smoother texture)

== Procedure ==
# Heat the [[Cookbook:oil|oil]] in a small pan over medium heat.
# Add minced garlic and [[Cookbook:Sautéing|sauté]] until golden.
# Add chopped tomatoes and cook until they soften.
# Add chile powder and salt. Stir well.
# [[Cookbook:Simmering|Simmer]] for 10–15 minutes until the mixture thickens.
# Add [[Cookbook:lemon juice|lemon juice]] or [[Cookbook:vinegar|vinegar]] if desired for extra tanginess.
# Let it cool before serving.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* For a smoother sauce, blend the mixture after cooking.
* Adjust the amount of chili to suit your spice tolerance.
* For a richer taste, roast the tomatoes before adding them.
* You can store shitha in a sealed jar in the refrigerator for up to one week.

text:
{{Recipe summary

}}{{Incomplete recipe|reason=missing appropriate linking, missing appropriate categories}}
{{Recipe}}


'''Shahan ful''' (also called '''ful''' or '''fūl''') is a traditional dish from Sudan and the Horn of Africa made from slow-cooked fava [[Cookbook:beans|beans]] mashed into a thick, savoury paste. It is commonly eaten in Sudan, Somalia, Eritrea, and Ethiopia, especially for breakfast, where it is served alongside tea, coffee, or fresh vegetables, and eaten by scooping the mixture with a flatbread such as injera.

==Ingredients==
* 2 cups dried fava beans (or canned fava beans)
* 1 medium onion, finely chopped
* 2 cloves garlic, minced
* 1 tomato, diced
* 1–2 green chilies, chopped
* 1 teaspoon ground cumin
* 1 teaspoon berbere spice (optional)
* 2 tablespoons olive oil or [[w:Niter kibbeh|niter kibbeh]]
* 1 tablespoon lemon juice
* Salt to taste
* Black pepper to taste
* Yogurt or feta cheese for serving (optional)
* Fresh coriander or parsley (optional)
* Bread rolls or flatbread for serving

==Equipment==
* Cooking pot
* Wooden spoon
* Knife
* Cutting board
* Bowl

==Procedure==
# Wash and soak the dried fava beans overnight.
# Drain the beans and place them in a large pot with fresh water.
# Simmer over low heat until the beans become soft and tender. Add more water if necessary.
# Mash the cooked beans into a coarse paste using a spoon or potato masher.
# In another pan, heat the olive oil or niter kibbeh over medium heat.
# Add the onions and cook until soft.
# Stir in the [[Cookbook:garlic|garlic]], tomatoes, chilies, cumin, and berbere spice.
# Cook for several minutes until fragrant.
# Add the mashed beans and stir well.
# Season with lemon juice, salt, and black pepper.
# Simmer for a few minutes until thick.
# Serve hot with yogurt, feta cheese, or fresh herbs if desired.

==Notes, tips, and variations==
* Soaking the beans overnight reduces cooking time.
* Slow cooking improves flavour and texture.
* Olive oil adds richness and aroma.
* Canned fava beans can be used for faster preparation.
* Extra chili peppers may be added for a spicier dish.

title: Cookbook:Simple Tarragon Quiche
text:
{{recipesummary|category=French recipes|servings=6|time=75 minutes|difficulty=2|Image=[[Image:Quiche Lorraine.jpg|300px]]}}
__NOTOC__
{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of France|Cuisine of France]]

A '''quiche''' is a [[Cookbook:Baking|baked]], [[Cookbook:Sweeteners|unsweetened]] [[Cookbook:Custard|custard]] [[Cookbook:Dessert#Pies, Tarts|pie]], often made with savory fillings. Originally served in Germany, quiche was adopted by neighboring France and is now considered a traditional French dish. The French (and now English) word ''quiche'' comes from a dialectal form (''Küchle'') of the German word for [[Cookbook:Dessert#Cakes, cupcakes|cake]] (''Kuchen''). Quiche became popular in Britain after World War II and in the United States during the 1960s and 70s.

==Ingredients==
*5 [[Cookbook:Egg|egg]]s
*1 ⅓ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] (320 [[Cookbook:mL|ml]]) [[Cookbook:Cream|cream]] (approximately 30% [[Cookbook:Oil and fat|fat]])
*1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]] fresh [[Cookbook:Tarragon|tarragon]]
*1 [[Cookbook:Dash|dash]] ground [[Cookbook:Nutmeg|nutmeg]]
*¼ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
*⅛ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] ground [[Cookbook:Pepper|pepper]]
*1 prepared frozen [[Cookbook:Pie Crust|pie crust]]
*¾ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] (180 [[Cookbook:mL|ml]]) freshly-[[Cookbook:Grating|grated]] [[Cookbook:Swiss Cheese|Swiss cheese]]

==Procedure==
#Preheat [[Cookbook:Oven|oven]] to [[Cookbook:Oven Temperatures|375°F]] (190°C).
#Place the eggs, cream, tarragon, nutmeg, salt, and pepper in a [[Cookbook:Blender|blender]]; blend ''as briefly as possible'' until they form a homogeneous mixture.
#In the pie crust, create alternating layers of the shredded cheese and the mixture from the blender until the crust is full.
#[[Cookbook:Baking|Bake]] the quiche for 35–40 minutes; a [[Cookbook:Skewer|toothpick]] or fork inserted into its middle should come out "clean".
#Remove the quiche from the oven, and let it cool for at least 20 minutes before serving.

==Notes, tips, and variations==
*Use nutmeg sparingly.
*Fresh tarragon will be better than dried tarragon.
*Placing a very hot pan in under the quiche will give it greater volume.
*Try making quiches with [[Cookbook:Sautéing|sautéed]] [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]]s, sautéed [[Cookbook:Broccoli|broccoli]], and shredded sharp [[Cookbook:Cheddar cheese|cheddar cheese]]; feel free to experiment.

==Warnings==
*The quiche mixture may drip over the edge of the pie crust while cooking; place it on a cookie sheet or place foil on the oven rack below it.
*The quiche will continue to cook after it is removed from the oven; be careful not to overcook it or cut it before it has had a chance to set.
*[[Cookbook:Half and Half|Half-and-half]] (cream with approximately 12% fat) can be substituted for regular cream to make this dish less fattening; however, be cautious of using milk because low-fat dairy products curdle more easily.

Commonly found in the Southern United States, '''skillet cornbread''' is delicious, easy to make, and often served beside a pot of brown beans. It can be made a day or two ahead of time, as long as care is taken to keep it from drying out.

==Ingredients==
*¾ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] white all-purpose [[Cookbook:Flour|flour]]

*1–2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] [[Cookbook:White sugar|white sugar]]
*¾ tsp [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
*1 ¼ cups yellow or white [[Cookbook:Cornmeal|cornmeal]]
*1 [[Cookbook:Egg|egg]]
*2–3 tbsp melted [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]] or [[Cookbook:Lard|pan drippings]]
*1 cup [[Cookbook:Milk|milk]] or [[Cookbook:Buttermilk|buttermilk]]

==Procedure==
#Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C)
#Grease the skillet with bacon drippings (ideal) or oil. Butter isn't recommended, since it can burn when you preheat the skillet.
#Preheat the skillet until the drippings/oil is smoking. This ensures a good crust on the bottom of the cornbread.
#In a bowl, sift together the flour, baking powder, sugar, and salt.  Thoroughly mix the sifted ingredients together and add the corn meal.
#In a second bowl, beat the egg well. Add the melted butter (or pan drippings) and the milk and continue to beat until well mixed.
#Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and mix using fast strokes. Take care not to overmix.
#Pour the batter into the skillet and place in the oven. Bake for 25-30 minutes. The cornbread should have a golden brown color when done, and a knitting needle or knife-point will come out "dry" when inserted in the bread.

==Notes, tips, and variations==
*Ideally, all ingredients should be at room temperature (about 75°F / 24°C) for this recipe. However, a good result can still be had if this is not the case.
*Yellow corn meal is preferable to white corn meal, but this can vary according to locality and personal taste.
*Optionally, ¼ to ½ cup of diced cooked ham or crumbled bacon can be added to the batter before pouring into the skillet. This may add a few minutes to the baking time.

==Warnings==
*The skillet must be oven-safe. Ideally, skillet cornbread should be baked in a cast-iron skillet.

title: Cookbook:Sinigang (Philippine Sour Soup)
text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Soup recipes
| Difficulty = 3
| Image = [[File:Sinigang na Baboy DSCF4234.jpg|300px]]
}}

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of the Philippines|Cuisine of the Philippines]]

'''Sinigang''', the famous sour soup of the [[Cookbook:Cuisine of the Philippines|Philippines]], is a fruity sour-based soup boiled with either pork, beef, chicken, fish or seafood. A variety of vegetables can be included, but onions and tomatoes are required. Root vegetables are too starchy and not recommended, with the exception of taro root, which adds a milky and starchy texture. Okra can also provide a pleasant thickness, although it is more clear or transparent. The most common souring agent for the soup is tamarind, but unripe mango, [[Cookbook:Calamansi|calamansi]] juice, unripe watermelon, starfruit, cane vinegar, citrus juice, guava, and kamias can also be used. The meat and tomato provide a savory umami flavor, while fatty meat tempers the sourness. Semi-hot chile peppers add mild spice and make the soup aromatic.

Sinigang was often compared to Tom Yam of Thailand, but Sinigang is more sweeter and lighter in spice, contrast to strong flavor of Thai variety. Some critics say Sinigang should be considered a national food of the Philippines, since it originates in the local cuisine.

== Ingredients ==
* Sampaloc ([[Cookbook:Tamarind|tamarind]]) fruits or ready-to-use tamarind paste
* 1 [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 4–6 [[Cookbook:Tomato|tomatoes]], quartered
* ½–1 [[Cookbook:Kilogram|kg]] [[Cookbook:Pork|pork belly]], cubed
* 250 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] [[Cookbook:Taro Root|taro]] root, diced or sliced into chunks
* 3–4 [[Cookbook:Horseradish|horseradish]], sliced
* 200 g [[Cookbook:String beans|string beans]], cut in 1-inch pieces
* 1–3 onions, quartered
* 250 g [[Cookbook:Kangkung|kangkung]] (water spinach) leaves or other leafy yet crunchy vegetable even when cooked.
* 5 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|Tbsp]] [[Cookbook:Fish Sauce|fish sauce]]
*Salt
*[[Cookbook:Pepper|Pepper]]
*[[Cookbook:MSG|MSG]] (optional)
*3 green [[Cookbook:Chiles|chiles]] (e.g. serrano or any other fragrant and mild variety)

== Procedure ==
# If using whole tamarind, boil it in water until the shells crack, then work the flesh away from the seeds and strain, reserving all the liquid for the soup. Skip this process if using packed tamarind base.
# [[Cookbook:Sautéing|Sauté]] the chopped onions in another large pot.
#Add the tomato and pork to the onions, and sauté until the pork is no longer pink.
#Add enough water or boiled tamarind stock to cover the contents of the pot. [[Cookbook:Boiling|Boil]] until tender.
#Add taro root, and [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] until soft and tender. The soup should to thicken at this point.
# Add the horseradish, and simmer until tender-crunchy.
# Add the string beans, quartered onions, and water spinach. Simmer for another 2–3 minutes.
# Check to make sure all ingredients were cooked enough, then add the tamarind pack if using.
#Add fish sauce, salt, pepper, and MSG to taste. Top with green chillies.
#Serve hot.

title: Cookbook:Simple Spaghetti
text:
{{recipesummary|category=Pasta recipes|servings=4|time=30 minutes|difficulty=1|image=[[File:Spaghetti served with meat sauce.jpg|300px]]}}
{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of Italy|Cuisine of Italy]] | [[Cookbook:Italian-American cuisine|Italian-American cuisine]]

== Ingredients ==
For 4 servings:
* 2.25 [[Cookbook:Liter|L]] (10 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]]) water
* 8 [[Cookbook:Ounce|oz]] (224 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]]) [[Cookbook:Spaghetti|spaghetti]]
* 2.5 cups (24 oz) pasta sauce (optional but recommended)
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]] (optional but recommended)
* [[Cookbook:Vegetable Oil|Vegetable oil]] (optional but recommended)

== Procedure ==

# On a stovetop, bring the water to a boil on high heat after adding salt and vegetable oil (see tips below).
# Reduce heat to medium and add the pasta.
# While the spaghetti is cooking, pour desired amount of sauce into pan and set stove to medium.
# Set a timer for 7 minutes. When the timer goes off, fish out a strand of spaghetti and bite into it.  What you're going for here is al dente, meaning that the pasta is just soft enough to eat: no longer crunchy in the middle, and not mushy and over-done. A more traditional (but messy) way to see if the spaghetti is done is to throw some strands onto a wall.  If they stick to the wall, then the pasta is ready to eat.
# When the sauce begins to bubble, reduce the heat to its lowest setting and cover. 
# Once the pasta is ready, carefully drain it through a colander into a sink. 
# Serve sauce over pasta in bowls.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* Adding salt to the cooking water enhances the pasta flavor and to allows the water to boil more quickly. Adding vegetable oil to the cooking water helps prevent the spaghetti from sticking together.
* Try adding herbs or fruit (such as [[Cookbook:Pineapple|pineapple]] tidbits) to the water before it boils to keep with the pasta after straining for extra flavor and texture.
* Before cooking the sauce, consider [[Cookbook:sauté|sauté]]ing some finely minced onions, [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]], ground [[Cookbook:Beef|beef]] (or [[Cookbook:Pork|pork]]/[[Cookbook:Sausage|sausage]]/[[Cookbook:Veal|veal]]/etc.), cheese ([[Cookbook:Parmesan Cheese|parmesan]]/[[Cookbook:Mozzarella Cheese|mozzarella]]/etc.), [[Cookbook:Mushroom|mushrooms]], or anything else that catches your fancy. Then add the sauce. 
* In a pinch, you can make plain spaghetti and add ketchup if you do not have any pasta sauce available.
* The following foods go well with spaghetti and can be served together:
** [[Cookbook:Broccoli|Broccoli]] (or other [[Cookbook:Vegetable|vegetables]]).
** [[Cookbook:Garlic Bread|Garlic Bread]]
** [[Cookbook:Meatballs|Meatballs]]
** [[Cookbook:Pineapple|Pineapple]] (or other [[Cookbook:Fruit|fruits]]) tidbits ([[Cookbook:Boiling|boiled]], [[Cookbook:Grilling|grilled]], or [[Cookbook:Frying|fried]])
** Shredded and/or grated [[Cookbook:Cheese|cheese]]
** [[Cookbook:Tomato Sauce|Tomato]], [[Cookbook:Alfredo Sauce|alfredo]], or other [[Cookbook:Sauces|sauces]] (can choose one, the other, or mixed together)
* Cooking is about experimentation—never be afraid to try anything once!

title: Cookbook:Simple Syrup
text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Syrup recipes
| Difficulty = 1
}}

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Sweeteners|Sweeteners]]

'''Simple syrup''', also known as sugar syrup or bar syrup, is a [[cookbook:sweeteners|sweetener]] made of sugar and water. It is often used to sweeten cold beverages, in which solid sugar will not readily dissolve. As its name suggests, simple syrup is very easy to prepare. Prepared syrup can be refrigerated for up to a week. It is 30% sweeter than table sugar.

==Ingredients==
*1 part [[cookbook:Water|water]]
*1–2 parts [[cookbook:Granulated Sugar|granulated sugar]]

==Procedure==
# Combine the sugar and cold water in a [[cookbook:saucepan|saucepan]].
# Bring the water to a boil over high heat, stirring constantly.
# When all of the sugar has dissolved, remove from the heat and allow to cool to room temperature. This should only take a few minutes.
# Transfer to a storage container, and refrigerate until needed.
==Notes, tips, and variations==
*Food coloring can be added to make differently colored syrups.
*Flavors and extracts can be added after the sugar dissolves, to create flavored syrups.
*The ratio of sugar and water can be changed to make thinner or thicker syrup. Alternately, one can add [[cookbook:pectin|pectin]] to make it gel.

* 1 [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] salt

#Combine salt, honey, and vinegar in a 6-quart container. Add ice, cover, and shake until ice is mostly melted and brine has cooled.

#Combine seasonings and sugar. Press into all sides of meat. Set aside.
#Preheat smoker to 200°F with the hickory chunks. Add roast, cover, and cook until internal temperature reaches 135°F for medium rare.
#Remove to a plate and cover tightly with [[Cookbook:Aluminium Foil|foil]]. Let rest 15 minutes before serving.

title: Cookbook:Smoked Eulachons
text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Fish recipes
| Difficulty = 3
}}

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Seafood|Seafood]]

'''Smoked eulachons''' is a common method for preparing eulachons. When smoked, eulachons provide an excellent source of fat, protein, iron, and riboflavin. Eulachon and eulachon grease are also an excellent source of vitamin A and omega-3 fatty acids.

== Ingredients ==

* Fresh [[Cookbook:Eulachon|eulachons]]
* Coarse [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]

==Procedure==

#Wash the eulachons well under running water.
#In a barrel, mix a brine solution of water and enough salt to make a potato float. A good ratio is 2 cups (500 ml) coarse salt in 3 gallons (12 litres) water. Add the fish.
#Soak for about ½–1 hour, or until the fish eyes turn white.
#Hang the eulachons for smoking by threading on cedar sticks. Push the strip of red cedar in through the gills and out through the mouth. Usually 12–25 eulachons are put on each stick.
#Hang the sticks from the rafters in a smokehouse, making sure the fish are not touching each other. There needs to be enough space between each rack and the fish so that the smoke is even.
#Let the fish finish dripping, then start the smoking fire with alder wood.
#Smoke the eulachon for 2–6 days. Smoke longer to make drier fish.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* Half-smoked eulachons (i.e., left one to two days in the smokehouse) may be canned for storage.

text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Soup recipes
| Servings = 1
| Difficulty = 1
}}

{{Recipe}}

This '''miso soup''' is a close approximation of what you get in most cheap western Japanese restaurants. All ingredients are to taste; the primary thing is the ratio of miso to dashi.

== Ingredients ==
* 250 [[Cookbook:Milliliter|ml]] (1 [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]]) [[Cookbook:Dashi|dashi]]
* 5 pieces of [[Cookbook:Wakame|wakame]]
* A few 1 [[Cookbook:Cm|cm]] cubes of medium-firm [[Cookbook:Tofu|tofu]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoon]] (about 15 ml) [[Cookbook:Miso|miso]] paste (either white, red, or a mixture)

== Procedure ==
# Heat the dashi to a light [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]].
# While this is heating, lay out your bowl and place the wakame and tofu in the bottom.
# When the dashi simmers, take a ladle or so of liquid aside and mix it with the miso paste.
# Remove the pot of dashi from the stove and stir in the miso mixture.
# Ladle the prepared soup into the bowl and serve.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* Some prefer less miso, some prefer more. The quantity given results in the moderately-salty type popular in restaurants before meals.

'''Sinasir''' is a rice [[Cookbook:Pancake|pancake]] popular in the northern part of Nigeria. It is made from cooked and soaked short-grained rice as used in ''tuwo shinkafa''.

==Ingredients==

==Procedure==

# Place the rice in a bowl, and cover it with about 1 inch of water. Soak for several hours.

# Heat a non-stick frying pan, and grease with a thin layer of oil.
# Scoop in enough batter to make a thin layer in the pan. Cook until the bottom is browned and the pancake is cooked through.

title: Cookbook:Simple Soup Dashi (Japanese Soup Stock)
text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Broth and stock recipes
| Difficulty = 2
}}

{{Recipe}}

This dashi can be used to make a miso soup similar to those served in restaurants in North America.

== Ingredients ==
* 3 large handfuls [[Cookbook:Bonito Flakes|dried, smoked, thinly-shaved skipjack tuna ''(katsuobushi)'']]
* 4–5 [[Cookbook:Each|ea]]. 4-inch (10 [[Cookbook:Centimetre (cm)|cm]]) long sheets of [[Cookbook:Konbu|kombu]] seaweed
* 4–8 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] (1–2 [[Cookbook:Liter|liters]]) water

== Process ==
# Cut small gashes into the kombu. Do not wash the kombu; the white powder on the exterior is actually natural, crystallized [[Cookbook:MSG|MSG]] and gives the soup flavour.
# Place the kombu into the water and bring it to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]], skimming the surface periodically
# Just as the water begins to [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]], remove the kombu (this may be re-infused with less water a second time to make a lower-quality dashi suitable for cooking)
# Let the stock cool down for approximately 5 minutes
# Add the flaked tuna and stir, returning to heat
# Permit it to boil for about 30 seconds and remove from heat
# After a few minutes, the fish will sink to the bottom. Strain the stock through a fine mesh filter ([[Cookbook:Cheesecloth|cheesecloth]] works well), squeezing the fish to extract every bit of juice (this may be re-infused as well)
# Store in the fridge for up to 5 days, and in the freezer for up to 6 months

title: Cookbook:Sockerdricka (Swedish Ginger Drink)
text:
__NOTOC__{{Recipe summary
| Category = Beverage recipes
| Difficulty = 2
}}

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of Sweden|Swedish recipes]]

'''Sockerdricka''' (Swedish for "sugar drink") is a soft drink from the 19th century. It is traditionally a [[Cookbook:Fermentation|fermented]] drink that contains ginger, but modern commercial versions consist of carbonated water, some sugar, and citric acid.

== Ingredients ==
* 20 [[Cookbook:Liter|litres]] [[Cookbook:Water|water]]
* Peel of 1 [[Cookbook:Lemon|lemon]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Kilogram|kg]] white granulated [[Cookbook:Sugar|sugar]]
* 60 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] [[Cookbook:Yeast|yeast]]
* 25 g [[Cookbook:Ginger|ginger]]
* [[Cookbook:Raisin|Raisins]]

== Procedure ==
# [[Cookbook:Boiling|Boil]] the sugar, water, lemon and crushed ginger for 15 minutes. 
# [[Cookbook:Straining|Strain]] the mixture and let it cool. 
# Mix in the yeast and let the mixture [[Cookbook:Fermentation|ferment]] for 2 days. 
# Put the drink in bottles, and add a raisin to each bottle.
# Cork the bottles, and let rest for 5 days. After 5 days the sockerdricka is ready for drinking.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* The recipe above has '''lots''' of yeast, and not much ginger. It would work well with just 10 g yeast. More ginger would be good (e.g. 100 g of fresh ginger for 20 litres).

==See also==
* [[Cookbook:Ginger beer|Ginger beer]]
* [[Cookbook:Sima|Sima]]

This is an Eurasian dish, not to be confused with the American dessert made with toasted marshmallows (s'mores).

==Ingredients==
=== Marinating ===

* ¼ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] [[Cookbook:Baking Soda|bicarbonate of soda]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] ground [[Cookbook:pepper|pepper]] 
* 1 teaspoon [[Cookbook:salt|salt]] 
* 1 teaspoon [[Cookbook:sugar|sugar]] 
* 2 tablespoons [[Cookbook:vinegar|vinegar]] 
* 4 tablespoons dark [[Cookbook:Soy Sauce|soya sauce]] 
* 2 tablespoons [[Cookbook:oil|oil]]
* 420 [[Cookbook:Milliliter|ml]] water

=== Cooking ===
* 3 [[Cookbook:onion|onion]]s 
* 5 cloves [[Cookbook:garlic|garlic]] 
* 1 thumb-sized piece [[Cookbook:ginger|ginger]], julienned
* 10 cm piece [[Cookbook:cinnamon|cinnamon]], rinsed
* 100 g small [[Cookbook:carrot|carrot]]s, peeled and [[Cookbook:Slicing|sliced]] diagonally 
* 3 [[Cookbook:potato|potato]]es, peeled and quartered
* 1 [[Cookbook:tomato|tomato]], quartered
* [[Cookbook:Spam|Spam]] (optional) 
* Chicken hot dogs (optional)
* 1 sprig [[Cookbook:Cilantro|coriander leaves]], leaves plucked

== Procedure == 
=== Marinating ===
# Wash and cut beef into 2.5 cm chunks. 
# Drain in [[Cookbook:Colander|colander]]. 
# Combine beef with bicarbonate of soda, pepper, salt, sugar, vinegar and dark soya sauce.
# Leave for 30 minutes to [[Cookbook:Marinating|marinate]].

=== Cooking ===
# Grind onions and garlic together.
# Soak carrots and potatoes in water.
# Heat oil in a pot. When hot, [[Cookbook:Frying|fry]] ground onion and garlic, shredded ginger, and cinnamon until the onions are brown and fragrant.
# Add marinated beef. Fry until meat changes color.
# Add water and [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] until meat is tender. Stir occasionally to prevent meat from sticking to pot. Add more water if gravy is too thick, and season accordingly. 
# Add carrots and cook for 5 minutes.
# Add potatoes and cook until soft.
# Add tomato. If you like, you may add a tin of Spam luncheon meat, cut into thick slices or chicken franks at this step.
# Garnish with coriander leaves and serve.

}}

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of Ontario|Cuisine of Ontario]] | [[Cookbook:Cookie|Cookies]]

This recipe for '''sugar cookies''' has been running with the Gilbert women of Ontario, Canada for more than 100 years. No one knows where the recipe started, but it's been that way as long as any can recall with no real change.

==Ingredients==
* 3 [[Cookbook:Egg|eggs]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] (230 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]]) [[Cookbook:Shortening|shortening]] or [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]]
* [[Cookbook:Vanilla|Vanilla]], to taste
* 1 cup (200 g) white granulated [[Cookbook:Sugar|sugar]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Pinch|pinch]] of [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] (10 g) [[Cookbook:Baking Powder|baking powder]]
* 2–3 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] (250–375 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]]) [[Cookbook:Flour|flour]]

==Procedure==
# In a large bowl, beat eggs lightly to break the yolks as one would for scrambled eggs, then mix in the shortening. If using butter, soften it slightly beforehand by heating it a little. The shortening/egg mixture should be loose.
# Mix in the sugar, then add the salt to the liquid mixture.
# Add the baking powder, then slowly add the flour as needed to reach a proper [[Cookbook:Dough|doughy]] state (in essence, able to be shaped without sticking to one's hands too much). You may not need all of the flour, or you may even need a little more based on your eggs and how closely you measured.
# Make balls and place onto a greased or [[Cookbook:Parchment Paper|parchment]]-lined pan then into an oven heated to 175°C (350°F), and let [[Cookbook:Baking|bake]] for between 15–20 minutes.

==Notes, tips, and variations==
* Feel free to switch out half the sugar with another sweet item, like [[Cookbook:Honey|honey]].
* Using three tablespoons of [[Cookbook:Cocoa Powder|cocoa powder]] one can get a slight chocolate flavour to the cookie, without being overtly chocolatey.
* Try adding [[Cookbook:Chocolate Chip|chocolate chips]] to the dough.
*Approximately 1 teaspoon of [[Cookbook:Vanilla|vanilla]] extract works well for this recipe.
*Adding some [[Cookbook:Cinnamon|cinnamon]] and [[Cookbook:Nutmeg|nutmeg]] gives a good flavor.
* When heating up the butter, make sure that it's only barely solid when it's mixed into the eggs.

* 1 stalk [[Cookbook:Green onion|green onion]] 
* 25 g [[Cookbook:Galangal|galangal]] 
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] cooking oil

==Procedure==
#Grind the ingredients for the spice paste together in a [[Cookbook:Food Processor|food processor]]. [[Cookbook:Stir-frying|Stir fry]] the spice paste over slow fire until fragrant. Remove from the heat.
#Make soup by cooking the whole chicken with spice paste, galangal, lime leaves, lemon grass, and bay leaves in a pot for at least 30 minutes until the meat is tender. Use a pressure cooker for faster cooking time and better broth. For a traditional method, bring soup to [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]], cover, and turn off heat, then let steep for 30–40 minutes—this makes the meat more tender.
#Add a little bit of salt or pepper to taste.
#Leave the chicken in a pot until the soup is cool.
#Remove the meat from the bones, and slice the meat into tiny bit size using fork and knife, then set aside.
#Put back the bones into the soup, add sliced green onion, and bring the soup to the boil right before serving.

==Serving==
#In a bowl, arrange in the following layers: sliced potatoes, sliced tomatoes, vermicelli, cabbage, bean sprouts, sliced egg, and the meat on top.
#Pour the boiling soup over the ingredients, but don't let any bones or chicken skin go into the bowl.
#Put fried shallots on top, and squeeze a slice of lemon over top.
#Serve with hot steamed rice or slices of lontong (steamed rice roll).

==Notes, tips, and variations==
* Many versions of soto ayam don't have tomato.
* Some prefer not to mix cabbage with bean sprouts.
* As fried potato substitute, some like to put potato chips into the soup.

title: Cookbook:Snickerdoodles IV
text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Cookie recipes
| Servings = 36
| Difficulty = 2
| Image = [[File:Snickerdoodles.jpg|300px]]
| Time = 60 minutes
}}

{{recipe}} | [[:Category:Cookie recipes|Cookies]]

'''Snickerdoodles''' are sugar cookies lightly dusted with [[Cookbook:cinnamon|cinnamon]]. They have a characteristically crackly surface, and can be crisp or soft, depending on preference. Some variants include nutmeg, raisins, or nuts. They are a traditional Christmas cookie in North America.

''The Joy of Cooking'' claims that snickerdoodles are probably German in origin, and that the name is a corruption of the German word for "snail noodles" (''schneckennudeln'').

== Ingredients ==

* 344 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] (2 ¾ [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] or 24 [[Cookbook:Ounce|oz]]) [[Cookbook:Flour|all-purpose flour]]
* ¼ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] [[Cookbook:Baking Soda|baking soda]]
* 2 tsp [[Cookbook:Cream of Tartar|cream of tartar]]
* 300 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] (1½ cups or 9 oz) [[Cookbook:Castor sugar|superfine sugar]]
* 110 g (½ cup or 4 oz) [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]]
*100 g (½ cup or 4 oz) [[Cookbook:Shortening|shortening]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Egg|eggs]]
* 1 tsp [[Cookbook:Vanilla|vanilla]] extract
* 3 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] [[Cookbook:Sugar|sugar]]
* 1½ tsp [[Cookbook:Cinnamon|cinnamon]]

== Procedure ==

# Preheat [[Cookbook:Oven|oven]] to [[Cookbook:Oven temperatures|350°F]].
# Mix flour, salt, baking soda, cream of tartar. Set aside.
# [[Cookbook:Beating|Beat]] butter, shortening and sugar.
# Beat in eggs and vanilla.
# Gradually add dry ingredients, mixing fully.
# Roll into 1 tbsp balls.
# Mix sugar and cinnamon.
# Roll balls in sugar-cinnamon mixture.
# Refrigerate for 30 minutes.
# [[Cookbook:Baking|Bake]] for 10 minutes or until crisp and light brown.
#Let cool completely before eating.

'''Smothered okra''' is an easy dish that works well as a side vegetable. It can also be added to seafood and okra [[Cookbook:Gumbo|gumbo]] as the okra base. It is made with [[Cookbook:Okra|okra]] and [[Cookbook:Tomato|tomatoes]], and is best served over [[Cookbook:Rice|rice]].

== Ingredients ==
* 1 [[Cookbook:Pound|lb]] (450 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]]) [[Cookbook:Okra|okra]], washed
* 4–5 medium [[Cookbook:Tomato|tomatoes]], [[Cookbook:Dice|diced]]
* ½ medium-large yellow [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], diced 
* 2–3 stalks [[Cookbook:Celery|celery]], [[Cookbook:Slicing|sliced]] or diced 
* 1 green [[Cookbook:Bell Pepper|bell pepper]], diced 
* 2–3 cloves [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]], sliced or diced
* 1 stick (½ [[Cookbook:Pound|lb]] / 113 g) [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]]
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]], to taste
* [[Cookbook:Pepper|Pepper]], to taste

==Procedure==
# Remove okra tips and heads, and slice into ¼–½ inch wide pieces.
# [[Cookbook:Sautéing|Sauté]] onion, celery, and bell pepper in butter until soft over medium heat, adding garlic to sauté shortly before the onion is soft.

# [[Cookbook:Simmering|Simmer]] over medium heat until the okra is no longer sticky and stringy. The okra will change to a darker green color.
# Serve over rice or freeze to use in your next gumbo.

'''Socca''' (French), '''torta di ceci''' or '''farinata''' (Italian), is a type of [[Cookbook:Flatbread|flatbread]] made from chickpea flour.

''See also: [[Cookbook:Calentita|Calentita]]''

==Ingredients==

* 300 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] (2 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]]) [[Cookbook:Chickpea Flour|chickpea flour]]
* 500 [[Cookbook:Milliliter|ml]] (2 cups) [[Cookbook:Water|water]]

==Procedure==
# Heat oven as high as it can go—around 300°C / 570°F is traditional, but do whatever your oven can manage that gets close to this. If using a cast-iron pan, get it into the oven at the start so that it is hot when the batter goes into it.
# [[Cookbook:Whisk|Whisk]] all the ingredients together well, ensuring there are no lumps. This should make a very thin, easy-to-pour batter.
# Once the oven is up to temperature, pour some of the batter into the hot pan or onto the plaque, and put into the oven for 8–9 minutes at 300°C / 570°F, or 13–15 minutes at 250°C / 480°F. With a 50 cm plaque or pan, cook half the batter at a time—the batter should cover the plaque or pan very thinly.
# Remove from the oven and cut into triangular wedges. Serve hot.
# Repeat for the rest of the batter.

title: Cookbook:Soft Boiled Eggs
text:
__NOTOC__{{Recipe summary
| Category = Egg recipes
| Difficulty = 1
| Image = [[File:Jajka na miękko-01.jpg|300px]]
}}

{{recipe}}

'''Soft-boiled eggs''' are a variety of whole boiled egg where the white is solid and the yolk is runny. They take about 7 minutes to prepare and are often served with buttered toast, perfect for dipping into the runny yolk.

==Ingredients==
*2–3 large [[Cookbook:Egg|eggs]], depending on appetite
*[[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]] (optional)

==Equipment==
*Small [[Cookbook:Saucepan|saucepan]]
*[[Cookbook:Cooktop|Stovetop]]
*A [[Cookbook:Slotted Spoon|slotted spoon]]
*A sharp pin or tack (optional)

==Procedure==

There are several popular ways to make soft-boiled eggs, and it is up to the cook to decide which method works best for them. Some of the most common ones follow.

=== Method 1 ===
This method boils the eggs continuously in the water.

# Bring a saucepan of water to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]].
# Gently add the eggs, and boil for 4–6 minutes (4 minutes for runny yolk, 5 minutes for soft yolk).
# Remove the eggs from the water.

===Method 2===
This method boils the egg for a brief period of time before letting it sit in hot water.
#Bring water to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]] in a saucepan. 
#Gently add the eggs, and boil for 1 minute.
#Remove the saucepan from the heat, and allow eggs to stand in the hot water for 5 minutes.
# Remove the eggs from the water.

=== Method 3 ===
This method does not boil the eggs at all, instead letting them sit in hot water for a longer period of time.
# Bring water to a rolling [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]] in a saucepan.
#Gently add the eggs, then immediately remove the pan from heat and cover it.
#Let the eggs sit for 8 minutes, then remove them.

=== Method 4 ===
This method uses steam to cook the whites firmly while still maintaining a perfectly cooked, runny yolk. It produces consistent results every time.
#Bring about 1 [[Cookbook:Inch|inch]] of water to a rolling [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]] in a saucepan. You want just enough water to create steam but not evaporate completely.
#Gently add the eggs, then cover with a lid.
#Let boil/[[Cookbook:Steaming|steam]] for 6–6½ minutes, depending on how runny you want the yolks.
#Immediately remove pot from heat, and drain the hot water.

== Serving ==
[[File:Egg (Explored 2015-11-02) - Flickr - Maria Eklind.jpg|thumb|Serve soft-boiled eggs in an egg cup, so that the interior does not leak out.]]
#To serve, place eggs in an egg cup, shot glass, or anything that will allow the egg to stay upright.
#Using a small spoon, repeatedly tap the top of the eggs until an area the size of the spoon is cracked
#Dig the spoon across the bottom of the cracked area to remove the top.
#Use the spoon to eat from the egg shell, and/or cut toast into strips and dip into the egg.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* Adding a bit of salt to the cooking water can help to quickly set the whites if the egg leaks during cooking.
* Running the cooked eggs under cold water will help stop the cooking process.
* Some people use a pin to poke a small hole on the larger end of the egg before boiling it. It is believed that this helps give the egg a smooth, round bottom, and some say the pinhole makes it easier to peel.
* Soft-boiled eggs can be carefully peeled as an alternative serving method.

== External links ==

* https://www.exploratorium.edu/cooking/eggs/explore-text.html

text:
{{Recipe summary
| Category = Soup recipes
| Difficulty = 3
}}

{{recipe}}

== Ingredients ==
* 2 cloves [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Green Onion|scallions]], [[Cookbook:Slicing|sliced]], plus more for garnish
* ¼ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] roughly-[[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]] [[Cookbook:Parsley|parsley]]
* ½ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] dried [[Cookbook:Thyme|thyme]]
* 1 medium [[Cookbook:Shallot|shallot]], sliced
* 1 scotch bonnet [[Cookbook:Chiles|chile]], stemmed and seeded
* Juice of 1 [[Cookbook:Lime|lime]], plus wedges for serving
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]], to taste
* Freshly-ground [[Cookbook:Pepper|black pepper]], to taste
* 1 [[Cookbook:Pound|lb]] [[Cookbook:Beef#Chuck|beef chuck]], cut into ½-[[Cookbook:Inch|inch]] pieces
* 2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] olive oil
* 8 cups beef [[Cookbook:Stock|stock]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Carrot|carrots]], cut into 1½-inch pieces
* 2 stalks [[Cookbook:Celery|celery]], cut into 1½-inch pieces
* 1 small [[Cookbook:Leek|leek]], trimmed, halved lengthwise and cut into 1½-inch pieces; rinsed
* 1 small yellow [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], cut into 1½-inch pieces
* 1 large Yukon gold [[Cookbook:Potato|potato]], peeled and cut into 1½-inch pieces
* 1 medium [[Cookbook:Turnip|turnip]], peeled and cut into 1½-inch pieces
* ½ small green [[Cookbook:Cabbage|cabbage]], cored and cut into 1½-inch pieces
* ½ small calabaza or kabocha [[Cookbook:Squash|squash]], cut into 1-inch pieces

== Procedure ==
# [[Cookbook:Puréeing|Purée]] garlic, scallions, parsley, thyme, shallots, chile, juice, salt and pepper, and ½ cup water in a [[Cookbook:Blender|blender]] until smooth; mix with beef in a bowl, cover with [[Cookbook:Plastic wrap|plastic wrap]], and refrigerate at least 4 hours or overnight.
# Remove beef from marinade and dry with [[Cookbook:Paper Towel|paper towels]]; set aside.
# Heat oil in a 8 [[Cookbook:Quart|qt]] [[Cookbook:Saucepan|saucepan]] over medium-high heat. Add beef; cook, turning as needed, until browned, about 8 minutes. Add stock and bring to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]]; reduce heat to medium, and cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is tender, about 1½ hours. Add carrots, celery, leeks, onion, potatoes, turnips, and cabbage; cook, slightly covered and stirring occasionally, until vegetables are tender, about 20 minutes.
# Meanwhile, bring squash and 2 cups water to a boil in a 2 qt saucepan over high heat; reduce heat to medium-low and cook, covered, until squash is tender, about 10 minutes. Drain, reserving ½ cup cooking liquid and transfer squash and liquid to a blender; purée until smooth and set aside. When vegetables are tender, uncover, and stir in reserved squash purée; cook, stirring occasionally, until soup is slightly thick, 5–10 minutes more
# Season soup with salt and pepper and serve with scallions and lime wedges.

{{recipe}}

Originally posted to Foodista by user Simmer + Sauce. Foodista recipes are released under a [http://www.foodista.com/static/legal CC-BY license].

==Ingredients==
*2 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] cooked [[Cookbook:Millet|millet]]
*1 cup [[Cookbook:Walnut|walnuts]], lightly toasted and finely [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
*5 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] extra-virgin [[Cookbook:Olive Oil|olive oil]], divided
*4 ears of [[Cookbook:Corn|corn]], off the cob
*1 bunch [[Cookbook:Green Onion|scallions]], thinly [[Cookbook:Slicing|sliced]]
*1 package riced [[Cookbook:Cauliflower|cauliflower]]
*1½ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|tsp]] [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]], divided
*2 packages gluten-free baked [[Cookbook:Tofu|tofu]], teriyaki flavor, diced into ¼-inch squares (optional)
*1–2 tsp [[Cookbook:Chipotle Pepper|chipotle pepper in adobo sauce]], chopped

*¼ tsp [[Cookbook:Pepper|black pepper]]

==Preparation==
#Cook the millet per the package instructions using water or vegetable stock. Once cooked, remove from the pan and place in a medium size mixing bowl. Set aside.
#Preheat the [[Cookbook:Oven|oven]] to 350°F. Lightly toast the walnuts until fragrant, about 8 minutes. Set aside to cool. When cool enough to handle, finely chop and add to the cooked millet.
#Place a large [[Cookbook:Sauté Pan|sauté pan]] oven medium-high heat. Add 1 tablespoon olive oil. When hot, but not smoking, add the corn. Add ½ teaspoon of salt and stir to incorporate. Cook until the corn is a vibrant yellow color, about 4–5 minutes. Add the scallions and cook an additional 30 seconds. Remove form the heat and place in the bowl with the millet.

#To serve, divide among serving bowls. [[Cookbook:Garnish|Garnish]] with sliced radishes and chopped chives. This grain bowl can be served at warm or at room temperature.

text:
{{Recipe summary

}}

{{Recipe}}

'''Soup du pecheur''' is a spicy and delicious dish eaten with attieke.

== Ingredients ==

* 5 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] [[Cookbook:Water|water]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Pound|lb]] slightly grated [[Cookbook:Crayfish|crayfish]]
* 4 medium-size [[Cookbook:Onions|onions]], finely [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
* 4 medium-size [[Cookbook:Tomato|tomatoes]], finely chopped
* 15 [[Cookbook:Djansang|djansang]] seeds
* 5 [[Cookbook:Bay Leaf|bay leaves]]
* 1 lb [[Cookbook:Shrimp|shrimp]]
* 4 medium-size [[Cookbook:Crab|crabs]], slightly grated
* 1 large [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]] bulb, grated
* 2 dry [[Cookbook:Lemongrass|lemongrass]] leaves
* 3 medium-size habanero [[Cookbook:Chiles|peppers]], neatly chopped
* 6 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] red palm [[Cookbook:Oil|oil]]
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]] to taste
* [[Cookbook:Black pepper|Black]] [[Cookbook:Black pepper|pepper]] to taste

* 2 lb [[Cookbook:Crayfish|crayfish]]
* 4 lb tilapia fish
* 2 chicken [[Cookbook:Dehydrated Broth|bouillon cubes]], crushed
* 750 grams attieke (cassava couscous)

== Procedure ==

# Put 4 cups water in a saucepan, then add the crayfish, onions, tomatoes, djansang seeds, bay leaves, shrimp, crabs, garlic, lemongrass, habanero pepper, red palm oil, salt, and black pepper to your desired taste. Leave it to [[Cookbook:Boil|boil]] for about 30 minutes over medium heat. Make sure that the onions and tomatoes are soft at this point.
# Remove and grind the tomatoes, onions, djansang seeds, and garlic. Return them to the pot along with the fish.
# Reduce the heat to low and add the bouillon cubes. Let it cook for about 25 minutes.
# In the meantime start preparing your attieke according to the package directions.
# When the cassava couscous is hot, add the remaining red oil and [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]] to your desire taste. Mix it very well until the couscous turns orange.
# Serve your soup with the attieke.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* When cooking the soup, avoid using high heat as this can make the soup to boil very quickly, resulting in breaking of the fish.

title: Cookbook:Soso (Coconut Rice)
text:
__NOTOC__{{Recipe summary
| Category = Rice recipes
| Difficulty = 2
}}

{{recipe}}

'''Soso''', also known as coconut rice, is a popular dish in various cuisines, particularly in Africa and the Caribbean. It is a flavorful rice dish that incorporates the rich and creamy taste of coconut milk. 

== Ingredients ==

* [[Cookbook:Water|Water]]
* 2 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] long-grain [[Cookbook:Rice|rice]]
* 1 can [[Cookbook:Coconut Milk|coconut milk]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
* 2–3 [[Cookbook:Pandan|pandan]] leaves (optional)
* 1–2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] [[Cookbook:Vegetable oil|vegetable oil]] (optional)

== Equipment ==

* Large pot with lid
* Cooking spoon
* [[Cookbook:Cooktop|Stovetop]]

== Procedure ==

# Rinse the rice thoroughly under cold water until the water runs clear. Drain any excess water.
# In a large pot, combine the rinsed rice, coconut milk, water, salt, and pandan leaves (if using). Stir well to combine. If desired, you can add vegetable oil at this stage to prevent the rice from sticking together.
# Place the pot over medium-high heat and bring the mixture to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]], stirring occasionally.
# Once it reaches a boil, reduce the heat to low, cover the pot with a tight-fitting lid, and [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] for about 15–20 minutes or until the rice is cooked and the liquid has been absorbed. Avoid lifting the lid while the rice is cooking to ensure even cooking.
# After the cooking time, remove the pot from the heat but keep it covered. Let it rest for an additional 5–10 minutes to allow the steam to finish cooking the rice.
# Fluff the rice with a fork to separate the grains and remove the pandan leaves if used.
# Serve the coconut rice hot.

title: Cookbook:Sosso-Ngondi (Ground Cassava Porridge)
text:
__NOTOC__{{Recipe summary
| Category = Porridge recipes
| Difficulty = 2
}}

{{recipe}}

'''Sosso-ngondi''' is a traditional West African dish made from ground cassava. It is a smooth, thick, and creamy porridge that is often enjoyed as a breakfast or a filling snack. This comforting dish is popular in many countries across the region and is loved for its simple yet satisfying flavors.

== Ingredients ==

=== Base ===
* 2 [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] grated [[Cookbook:Cassava|cassava]] (fresh or frozen and thawed)
* 4 cups [[Cookbook:Water|water]]
* 1 cup [[Cookbook:Coconut Milk|coconut milk]] (or regular [[Cookbook:Milk|milk]] for a non-dairy alternative)
* ¼ cup white granulated [[Cookbook:Sugar|sugar]] (adjust to taste)
* ½ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] ground [[Cookbook:Cinnamon|cinnamon]]
* 1 [[Cookbook:Pinch|pinch]] of [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]

=== Toppings ===
* Shredded [[Cookbook:Coconut|coconut]]
* Sliced [[Cookbook:Banana|bananas]]
* [[Cookbook:Chopping|Chopped]] [[Cookbook:Nuts and Seeds|nuts]]
* [[Cookbook:Honey|Honey]]

== Equipment ==

* Large bowl
* Fine-mesh [[Cookbook:Sieve|strainer]] or [[Cookbook:Cheesecloth|cheesecloth]]
* [[Cookbook:Blender|Blender]] or [[Cookbook:Food Processor|food processor]]
* Medium-sized [[Cookbook:Saucepan|saucepan]]
* Wooden spoon or [[Cookbook:Spatula|spatula]]

== Procedure ==
# Place the grated cassava in a large bowl and add water. Use your hands to mix and squeeze the cassava to release the starch. Continue this process until the water becomes cloudy, and the cassava particles settle at the bottom of the bowl.
# Pour the cassava mixture through a fine-mesh [[Cookbook:Sieve|strainer]] or [[Cookbook:Cheesecloth|cheesecloth]] placed over another bowl, reserving the liquid. Let the mixture rest and allow the starch to settle at the bottom. This starch is what you'll use to make the porridge. Carefully pour off the water and keep the starch.
# Transfer the cassava starch to a [[Cookbook:Blender|blender]] or [[Cookbook:Food Processor|food processor]]. Add the coconut milk, sugar, ground cinnamon, and a pinch of salt. Blend until you achieve a smooth and creamy consistency.
# Pour the blended mixture into a medium-sized [[Cookbook:Saucepan|saucepan]]. Heat the mixture over medium heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon or spatula to prevent lumps and sticking.
# As the porridge cooks, it will thicken. Continue stirring until it reaches your desired consistency. It should be smooth and creamy, similar to the texture of oatmeal or grits.
# Remove it from the heat. Serve the warm porridge in bowls and top with shredded coconut, sliced bananas, chopped nuts, or a drizzle of honey.

title: Cookbook:Sombi
text:
{{Incomplete recipe|reason=missing links; missing categories; headings need to be corrected; sections need proper formatting}}{{Recipe summary
| Cuisine = Senegalese
| Origin = USA, 2010s
| Servings = 5
| Time = 30 minutes

'''Sombi''' is a traditional West African dish, especially popular in Senegal. Made with rice and coconut milk, it is served as a creamy, mildly sweet porridge or dessert.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lois |date=2015-04-16 |title=Senegalese Sombi: An Easy Coconut Rice Pudding |url=https://www.yummymedley.com/sombi-senegalese-coconut-rice-pudding/ |access-date=2025-07-27 |website=Yummy Medley |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-11-18 |title=Senegalese Sombi: A Coconut Rice Pudding |url=https://madinacuisine.wordpress.com/2018/11/18/senegalese-sombi-a-coconut-rice-pudding/ |access-date=2025-07-27 |website=Madina'Cuisine (All about african Foods) |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Sombi {{!}} Traditional Rice Pudding From Senegal {{!}} TasteAtlas |url=https://www.tasteatlas.com/sombi |access-date=2025-07-27 |website=www.tasteatlas.com}}</ref> This recipe is adapted from [https://www.saveur.com/article/recipes/senegal-coconut-rice-pudding/ one by Saveur magazine]. 
==Ingredients==
*4 cups [[Cookbook: Coconut Milk|coconut milk]]
* 1 cup unsweetened shredded [[Cookbook: Coconut|coconut]] (fresh or dried)
*½ cup packed light or dark brown [[Cookbook: Sugar|sugar]]
*½ teaspoon [[Cookbook: Kosher|kosher]] [[Cookbook: Salt|salt]]
*1 [[Cookbook: Vanilla|vanilla bean]] (seeds scraped and reserved)
*2 cups cooked white [[Cookbook:Rice|rice]]
*2 tablespoons fresh [[Cookbook: Lime|lime juice]]

==Procedure==
1. In a medium saucepan over medium heat, combine the coconut milk, shredded coconut, brown sugar, salt, and vanilla bean seeds. Bring the mixture to a gentle boil, stirring frequently. Cook for about 5 minutes, or until slightly reduced.

2.Add the cooked white rice and continue to stir. Cook for another 5 minutes, or until the rice begins to break down and the mixture thickens into a porridge-like consistency.

3.Remove the saucepan from heat and stir in the fresh lime juice.

4.Serve hot as a warm, mildly sweet dessert or breakfast porridge.
== Notes and tips==
The main ingredients are very important because they give the dish its real, traditional taste. To make it taste right, be sure to use good quality coconut milk, vanilla, and other fresh ingredients.

If you drink a lot of soda, host many parties with soda, or own a carbonating machine, you can save money by using '''generic soda extracts'''. Making soda from extract often costs less than a third of the price of purchasing soda in bulk. This recipe is adapted from Cartoon Cuisine.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Duck |first=Eats Like A. |date=2017-05-31 |title=Marge's Homemade Pepsi |url=https://www.cartooncuisine.com/the-simpsons/marges-homemade-pepsi/ |access-date=2025-11-17 |website=Cartoon Cuisine |language=en-CA}}</ref> 

If you use a soda extract containing caffeine, do not add more than three times more than the proportion listed here (when scaling up or down) to avoid a caffeine overdose.  

== Ingredients ==

* ½ [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] (7.5 [[Cookbook:Liter|ml]]) soda extract
* 1 [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] (240 ml) water
* 1 cup (240 ml) [[Cookbook:White sugar|white sugar]]
* 2 L [[Cookbook:Carbonated Water|carbonated water]]

== Procedure ==

# [[Cookbook:Boiling|Boil]] the soda extract, water, and sugar together to make a syrup of about 10 [[Cookbook:Ounce|oz]] (300 ml). 
# Mix the syrup with the carbonated water to make the finished soda.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* Use water from a carbonating machine or a brand of pure carbonated water such as Polar Original Sparkling Water, Great Value Seltzer Water, or Signature Select Seltzer Water. Do not use a brand of mineral water such as Perrier, San Pellegrino, or Mineragua because the added minerals will ruin the taste. Avoid flavored sparkling water such as La Croix or Spindrift because the preexisting fruit flavors will ruin the drink.

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of Germany|Cuisine of Germany]]

'''Spaetzle''' (German: ''Spätzle'') means literally translated "little sparrow" and is a Swabian specialty from Germany. It is made from flour, eggs, water, and salt. There are different techniques to make spaetzle, such as using a spaetzle-maker or spaetzle-press. The original technique is to use a kitchen board and a grater.

Spaetzle are served as side dishes with a [[Cookbook:Sauce|sauce]] to [[Cookbook:Meat and Poultry|meat]] or as main menu with [[Cookbook:Cheese|cheese]] and [[Cookbook:Onion|onions]].

== Ingredients ==
* 500 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] [[Cookbook:Flour|flour]]
* 5 [[Cookbook:Egg|eggs]]
* 150–200 [[Cookbook:mL|ml]] water
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]]

== Procedure ==
[[Image:Spätzlepresse2.jpg|thumb|Spaetzle-press in action|308x308px]]
# Combine all ingredients using hands or an electrical mixer.
# Add enough water to make a dough that is slightly sticky, but still elastic and stiff.
# Beat long enough for bubbles to rise.
# Boil a large pot with salted water.
# If using only a board, sweep a spoon of dough over the kitchen board with the grater. Cut/grate small pieces of the dough with the grater into the hot water. If using a spaetzle-maker, put a spoon of dough into the maker and press through the holes into the water. The spaetzle are done when they rise and swim on the water surface.
# Remove spaetzle from the water with a slotted spoon and put into a lightly oiled bowl.

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of India|Indian recipes]]

'''Mudde''' is a compact ball [[Cookbook:Swallow|swallow]] made from finger millet. It is a lunchtime staple of rural communities in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh in South [[Cookbook:Cuisine of India|India]], and an important source of long-lasting energy among the rural poor.

Serving immediately is preferable, but the balls can also be packed and eaten cold later. Before eating, if desired, poke a hole in the ball with your finger and pour in a little ghee. Dip pieces of the ragi dough in a watery sauce like [[Cookbook:Upeseru|upeseru]] broth and swallow; do not attempt to chew. Eat along with the solid upeseru for a complete meal that will keep you going all day.

==Ingredients==
* 2 ½ [[Cookbook:Cup|cups]] ''ragi'' (finger [[Cookbook:Millet|millet]]) flour
* 5 cups [[Cookbook:Water|water]]
* [[Cookbook:Ghee|Ghee]]

==Procedure==
# [[Cookbook:Boiling|Boil]] the water in a pot, add a little of the flour to make a paste, then add the rest of the flour.
# Stir once with the handle of a wooden spoon and leave it in the pot.
# Keep on low heat for about 10 minutes until it smells cooked.
# Stir until the mixture turns dark reddish-brown. Once it begins to leave the sides of the pot, remove the pot from the fire and stir vigorously for 5–10 minutes—it's hard work, but the longer you keep at it, the lighter it will be.
# Pull the mixture out and form into balls of about fist size.

title: Cookbook:Southwestern Scramble
text:
{{recipesummary|category=Breakfast recipes|servings=4|time=15 minutes|difficulty=2}}

{{recipe}}| [[Cookbook:Cuisine of the United States|United States]] | [[Cookbook:Breakfast|Breakfast]]

A '''Southwestern Scramble''' is a  scrambled eggs recipe with many spicy ingredients, such as onions and chilis. For a complete breakfast, serve with sliced, fried [[Cookbook:Wiejska|wiejska]] ([[Cookbook:Cuisine of Poland|Polish]] [[Cookbook:Sausage|sausage]]), [[Cookbook:Toast|toast]], and [[Cookbook:Orange|orange juice]].

==Ingredients==
*8 [[cookbook:Egg|egg]]s
*2 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tbsp]] (30 [[cookbook:mL|ml]]) [[Cookbook:Milk|milk]]
*[[Cookbook:Butter|Butter]], [[Cookbook:Margarine|margarine]], or [[Cookbook:Cooking Spray|cooking spray]], for [[Cookbook:Frying Pan|frying pan]]
*1 medium red [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]]
*1 medium green [[Cookbook:Chili Pepper|chile pepper]], such as [[Cookbook:Jalapeño|jalapeño]], seeded and chopped
*1 green [[Cookbook:Bell Pepper|bell pepper]], seeded and [[Cookbook:Slicing|sliced]]
*[[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]], to taste
*[[Cookbook:Pepper|Black pepper]], to taste
*Serve with [[Cookbook:Hot Sauce|hot sauce]], such as [[Cookbook:Tabasco Sauce|Tabasco sauce]]

==Procedure==
#Crack the eggs into a large mixing bowl, add the milk, and [[Cookbook:Beating|beat]] until well combined.
#Place a large [[Cookbook:Frying pan|frying pan]] over medium heat, add the butter, margarine, or cooking spray, and allow to melt. Add the onions, chili, and bell pepper, and [[Cookbook:Sautéing|sauté]] for 2–4 minutes.
#Add the eggs to the pan, and allow to cook for 30 seconds to 1 minute, until they just begin to set.
#Turn the heat up to high, and begin scrambling the eggs by scraping the bottom of the pan with a spatula and folding the cooked egg into the egg mixture.
#When the eggs are still moist, but mostly cooked, remove from the fire and plate.  
#Serve while still hot.

==Notes, tips, and variations==
*To adjust the spiciness, use more or fewer chili peppers, or use types varying levels of heat.
*The chilis are seeded because of the intense heat in the seeds, where the majority of the spicy capsaicin is. The seeds can be left in, but the scramble will be much hotter.
*Be sure to scrape the entire bottom of the pan, as well as the sides. Otherwise, those areas where the egg is not scraped will burn.
*Carryover heat will continue to cook the eggs, so they should be removed from the fire while still slightly underdone, or they will be overcooked.

title: Cookbook:Soy Milk I
text:
__NOTOC__{{Recipe summary
| Category = Beverage recipes
| Yield = 2 L
| Difficulty = 2
| Image = [[File:Soy milk (2).jpg|300px]]
}}

{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Vegan cuisine|Vegan cuisine]]
== Ingredients ==
*125 [[Cookbook:Gram|g]] dried [[Cookbook:Soy|soybeans]]
*About 3.5 [[Cookbook:Liter|L]] water

== Equipment ==

*Hand [[Cookbook:Blender|blender]]
*Large pot with, ideally, a transparent lid
*Large can to hold the milk
*Wooden spoon or another tool for stirring
*Clean [[Cookbook:Cheesecloth|cheesecloth]] or dish cloth
*Sealable container for the okara (optional, you can also elect to dump or compost it, or [[Cookbook:Tempeh|ferment it]])

== Procedure ==

#Put the soybeans and 1 L of water into the pot, and let them soak for 8–12 hours.
#Strip the soaked beans of their hulls by rubbing or crushing them between your fingers. Remove the hulls and pour away the excess water. While the hulls have about the same density as the beans and bean splinters, you can exploit their high flow resistance for separating the two: Fill some water into the bowl, then pour it away quickly enough to drag the hulls with it, but not so quickly that the beans will follow. This process resembles the winnowing of dry chaff from seeds. It's no problem if a few hulls remain.
#Add ½ L of fresh water and [[Cookbook:Puréeing|blend]] until you get a creamy substance. Add another ½ liter and blend until totally smooth.
#Bring the raw milk to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]] while stirring, then reduce the temperature to minimum, put the lid on top, and [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] for 20 minutes. Attention: May overboil, check frequently. Removing the lid will allow vapor to escape and reduce the foam. Another possibility is to pour a little bit of cold water on top of the lid.
#The bitter odor of the raw milk should now be gone. Remove the pot from the stove and add 1 liter of cold water.
#Line the inside of the can with the cheesecloth so it is completely covered, and the edges of the cloth hang over the edge of the can. The following process will not work if the body of the can is much wider than the opening, though. In this case, use a large bowl instead.
#Carefully pour the cooked, unfiltered milk into the can. Then fold the cheesecloth together at the top and lift it up out of the can so that the filtered milk drips into the can. Rotate the bottom of the cloth against the top and use your hands to exert additional pressure upon the soy mass. Be careful not to burn yourself.
#When you're no longer able to extract significant amounts of milk from the soy mass, open the cheesecloth, and put the resulting rubberlike, crumbly [[Cookbook:Okara|okara]] ball into the prepared container. Store it in a cool place for up to 3 days; you may also freeze it.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==

* The soy milk can be kept in the refrigerator for about 5 days. You can also use it to make [[Cookbook:Tofu|tofu]] right away.
* The [[Cookbook:Okara|okara]] requires much more heat processing than the milk in order to be digestible. Boil it or [[Cookbook:Baking|bake]] it for at least one hour before eating it. The heat exposure during the baking of bread which contains okara is usually enough. Alternatively, it can be fermented into a special variety of [[Cookbook:Tempeh|tempeh]].
